title: Data model and BI
description: How flat extracts turn into a model a report can compute correctly and fast. Star schema, grain, evaluation context, time intelligence. The anchor is the PL-300 exam, but the order follows the logic of mistakes, not the exam syllabus.

intro.what:
A data model isn't a report file — it's a layer between raw tables and what a person sees on a dashboard: facts and dimensions laid out so the same measure computes correctly under any slice someone asks for. DAX is the language that measure is written in; it exists only inside a model and means nothing outside one, unlike SQL or Python code, which work on their own.

The main difference from SQL and pandas: there, you write a new query for every new question. Here, you build the model and its measures once, and after that any slice — by region, by month, by brand — the report computes on its own, with no new query.
intro.where:
A dashboard that different people open every day and slice differently — today by region, tomorrow by product group — and the number has to agree both times without hand-editing the query for each slice. A report built on a single flat extract, where joining the fact to a lookup table multiplied rows and quietly doubled revenue: a model with correctly set relationships and cardinality keeps that from happening structurally, not because whoever built the extract was careful enough.

At a BI-analyst interview this doesn't come up as DAX syntax trivia — it comes up as walking through an actual model: why did this double, why does a measure give the wrong thing under a slice, where should this column have lived. The same style of reasoning underlies the PL-300 exam, which this track uses as its anchor for topic coverage.
intro.idea:
A measure doesn't store a number — it gets computed at the moment the report already knows which slice is asking for it: that's the filter context. The same formula written as a calculated column computes once, at data refresh, and freezes — a measure recomputes for every cell of a pivot table, with its own set of filters from rows, columns and slicers.

That's where CALCULATE comes from — not an analogue of WHERE, but a tool that changes the filter context already in place, before the formula ever sees it. Until that difference settles, time intelligence (YTD, comparison to the prior period) looks like a set of spells to memorise; after it, the same one action applied to different date filters.
intro.limits:
DAX means nothing without a model around it: a formula relies on relationships between tables, and cut off from them it's just text. The model itself, though, travels — the same language and the same mechanics work in Power BI, in Power Pivot inside Excel, and in Analysis Services, so the skill is learned once, not relearned per tool.

A model doesn't replace SQL and pandas: it takes facts and dimensions that are already prepared, not raw data — if the source is dirty, that gets cleaned earlier, before the model.

And it isn't free: every extra relationship, every extra high-cardinality column, every extra calculated column grows the model and slows the report down. Later in the track we work through what's worth its cost and what didn't need to go into the model at all.
intro.bridge:
The same working question as in SQL, domain and pandas: the «Nettora» brand's revenue falling by nearly half. Here the same number is packaged as a measure that recomputes on its own under any slice — by region, by month, by channel — with no new query and no dataframe rebuilt for every new question.

If a measure, a query and a dataframe on the same data suddenly disagree, that's — as everywhere in this trainer — not a difference between tools, but a mistake in one of the three.

skills.title: Why analytics needs its own model
skills.summary: I understand why a report isn't built on the production database, and how a write-friendly schema differs from a read-friendly one.

skills.title: Fact grain
skills.summary: I can state in words what one fact row means, and I notice when a report mixes tables at different levels of detail.

skills.title: Star and snowflake
skills.summary: I split data into a fact and dimensions, and explain why one wide flat table is more expensive to maintain, not simpler.

skills.title: Relationships and cardinality
skills.summary: I set relationships with the right cardinality and always know which way a filter will flow through one.

skills.title: Two paths to the same table
skills.summary: I notice when there's more than one path from a fact to a dimension, and I know the model doesn't pick the best one for me in that case — it refuses to decide.

skills.title: Measure or calculated column
skills.summary: I choose deliberately between a measure and a column: a column computes once at refresh and takes up memory, a measure computes at query time and adapts to the slicer.

skills.title: Filter context
skills.summary: For any report cell I can list every filter acting on it: from rows, from columns, from slicers, and from the measure itself.

skills.title: Row context
skills.summary: I understand why SUM inside a calculated column returns the table's total, not the current row's value.

skills.title: Measure additivity
skills.summary: I tell apart measures that sum across any breakdown, semi-additive ones like stock on hand, and non-additive ones like shares, averages and prices.

skills.title: The date table
skills.summary: I keep a separate calendar in the model and can explain why filtering by date straight off a fact table is a dead end.

skills.title: One date, two roles
skills.summary: I connect the calendar to a fact table with two dates so a report by order date and by ship date computes off one date table, not two copies.

skills.title: Many-to-many and the bridge table
skills.summary: I recognize a many-to-many relationship by the key being non-unique on both sides, and resolve it with a bridge instead of joining directly and getting inflated sums.

skills.title: CALCULATE: replacing context
skills.summary: I read CALCULATE not as WHERE but as replacing filter context, and predict what happens to filters a slicer has already applied.

skills.title: Context transition
skills.summary: I explain why a measure invoked inside a table row computes something different from the same formula written as a column.

skills.title: Time intelligence
skills.summary: I compute YTD, a rolling year, the prior period and its growth — and understand what each of these functions does to the date filter.

skills.title: Power Query and the preparation layer
skills.summary: I decide where to clean data — at the source, in Power Query, or in a measure — and I do not push cleaning into DAX out of habit.

skills.title: Slowly changing dimensions
skills.summary: I can answer "which region did this customer belong to at the time of the sale", not just "which region are they in now".

skills.title: Incremental refresh
skills.summary: I set refresh up so the model does not reread the entire history every night for the sake of the last week.

skills.title: Model size and speed
skills.summary: I know that what bloats a model is column cardinality, not row count, and I remove what nobody will ever ask for.

tasks.title: Let the report read the live database
tasks.brief: You ask for data access for a dashboard. The developer offers to grant read-only straight into the production database: "the schema is already there, why build another one."
tasks.goal: Work out what will show up first.
tasks.scenario:
Production DB of an online store.
Daytime: checkout, payment.

Dashboard: revenue by category
over two years, refreshed every 5 min.

Orders in the DB: 4M rows
Concurrent shoppers: up to 300
tasks.predictQuestion: What will show up first?
hints: Ask exactly what the dashboard and the register compete for. Both hit the same hardware.
"Read-only" limits permissions, not load. Reading four million rows is an expensive operation on its own.
tasks.explain: An OLTP database is tuned for writes: short queries, each touching a handful of rows. An analytical query is built the opposite way — it reads a lot, rarely, and its cost is measured in volume scanned, not rows touched. Put them in one database and you don't get the sum of the two loads, you get contention: the report slows down checkout, and checkout slows down the report. That's exactly why a separate layer sits between a source and a report — one that refreshes on a schedule and lives its own life. The word "read-only" isn't an argument in this conversation: it's about permissions, not the cost of a query.

options.label: Recalculating the dashboard starts competing for resources with checkout, and shoppers will hit delays
options.why: A two-year query across four million rows reads about half the table, and it does that every five minutes. The production database is busy at that exact moment doing the thing that makes money. Read-only doesn't save you: the right to "only read" doesn't mean "read for free" — the contention is over disk, memory and CPU.

options.label: The dashboard will show wrong numbers, because the production database has no history
options.why: The history is right there — two years of orders haven't gone anywhere. The problem isn't completeness of data, it's that it has to be read from the same place new data is being written. Wrong numbers will show up later, for a different reason: the source's structure changes to fit the application's needs.

options.label: There won't be enough disk space: the dashboard will start creating temp tables
options.why: Space is the cheapest of the problems, and usually not the first one. A heavy analytical query hits CPU and disk reads long before the disk itself runs out. Naming this as the first risk means preparing for the wrong thing.

options.label: Nothing will break: read-only access can't change data
options.why: It really won't change data — but an incident isn't only about corrupted data. Slowing down the production database during peak hours costs the business more than a wrong number on a report, and it happens without a single error in the logs.

tasks.title: Five tables for one category
tasks.brief: You open the source schema to see where to pull the product category from for a report. The category turns out to be a tree, not a column.
tasks.goal: Work out why the source is structured this way.
tasks.scenario:
Source schema:

  order_lines → products
  products → product_categories
  product_categories → cat_tree
  cat_tree → cat_tree (parent)

To get «Beverages», you have to
walk the tree up to the root.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why is the source built this way, and why is it awkward for a report?
hints: Ask what this schema optimizes for. It has an intended reader, and it isn't the analyst.
Compare two operations: "rename a category" and "read the category for a million rows." Normalization makes exactly one of them cheap.
tasks.explain: Normal forms exist so data can't be corrupted by a partial edit: if a category name lives in one place, it can't drift from itself. The price is a join on every read. Reporting has the opposite priorities: data refreshes once a day, in full, but gets read constantly, in large chunks — so the dimension gets denormalized back: category becomes a column on the product lookup table. That's not "simplifying for analysts", it's a different set of trade-offs for a different workload. It follows that turning a source into a model is its own job, not just copying tables across.

options.label: It's cheaper to change this way: editing a category touches one row. A report needs the opposite — read everything at once — and every hop up the tree makes that more expensive
options.why: Normalization optimizes for writes: one change in one place, no copies to drift apart. A report lives by different rules — it reads millions of rows at once, and every join on that path multiplies by volume. What makes writing cheap makes reading expensive, and the other way around.

options.label: The source is designed wrong: the category tree should have been stored as one column
options.why: For the application it's actually the right call. The tree lets you add a subcategory without touching products, and guarantees the category name exists in exactly one place. The mistake isn't the source schema — it's trying to build a report on it with no layer in between.

options.label: The only difference is how fast the query is to write: the result is the same, the SQL is just longer
options.why: Query length is the smallest of the costs. A recursive climb up the tree for every fact row costs execution time, not writing time. And you'd have to repeat that logic in every new report that touches category — with the risk that it ends up different in two places.

tasks.title: The column got renamed overnight
tasks.brief: In the morning the dashboard greets you with an error. Overnight the app team shipped a release that renamed the status column to order_status — nobody thought about reporting.
tasks.goal: Work out what actually needs to change here.
tasks.scenario:
The dashboard reads the source
directly.

Before:  orders.status
After:   orders.order_status

Reports that reference it: 14
There was no warning.
tasks.predictQuestion: What actually needs fixing here?
hints: Don't ask "whose fault" — ask "why did one change cost fourteen fixes."
Compare two options: agreeing the source won't change, versus arranging things so its changes only touch one place.
tasks.explain: This shows the second argument for a separate model, besides load: decoupling in time and in ownership. The source belongs to the application team and changes on its schedule — that's correct and it won't change. As long as reports read it directly, each one is a hidden dependency the source's authors don't know about. A preparation layer makes that dependency explicit and singular: it breaks, not fourteen reports, and it gets fixed in one place by someone who understands why the column matters to reporting. Release sign-off doesn't solve the same problem, because it rests on people remembering, not on how the system is built.

options.label: That fourteen reports know the source structure directly. A preparation layer would have reduced the fix to one place
options.why: Renaming a column is ordinary life for an application — you can't forbid it. The defect isn't the release, it's that every report keeps its own copy of knowledge about the source schema: one change over there turns into fourteen fixes over here. A layer in between turns that into one.

options.label: The release process: developers must clear any schema change with analytics first
options.why: Sign-off looks like a solution and works like a tax: it slows the app team down for the sake of a consumer they shouldn't have to think about. And it rests on people remembering — the first change made in a hurry slips through. A technical seam is more reliable than an agreement.

options.label: Nothing: it's a one-off accident, fixing the fourteen queries is enough
options.why: It only looks like a one-off the first time. The source schema will keep changing — that's its normal behaviour, not a malfunction. Fixing the fourteen queries just returns the system to the exact state it already broke from once.

tasks.title: What one row means
tasks.brief: The first question for an unfamiliar fact table: what does one of its rows mean. The requester asks to "count the number of purchases for the quarter."
tasks.goal: Work out what a fact_sellout row describes, and whether the question can be answered.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellout — 118,449 rows

  week_start   week
  customer_id  outlet
  product_id   SKU
  units        units sold
  revenue      revenue

Distinct combinations of
"week × outlet × SKU": 118,449
tasks.predictQuestion: What does one row of this table mean?
hints: Compare two numbers: rows in the table, and distinct combinations of the key columns.
If a row meant one purchase, how many rows would there be for one SKU at one outlet in a week?
tasks.explain: Grain is checked by counting, not by reading column names: the row count should match the count of distinct combinations of the dimensions you consider the key. If it matches, the description is exact. If there are more rows, the grain is actually finer, and there's something in the key you haven't named. The practical takeaway matters more than the answer itself: this table has no answer to "how many purchases", because receipts are already summed inside it. That question should go back to the requester, not get swapped for the row count — which answers something else.

options.label: Total sales of one SKU at one outlet for one week — the match between row count and combination count confirms it
options.why: The match is the proof: if a row meant something finer-grained, the same combination would appear several times and there would be fewer distinct combinations than rows. Since the numbers are equal, the key isn't duplicated and the grain has been named exactly.

options.label: One purchase: one person buying one item
options.why: Then there would be many rows per SKU at one outlet in a week — one per receipt. Distinct "week × outlet × SKU" combinations would be noticeably fewer than 118,449, and they match the row count exactly. This table can't answer "how many purchases" at all — the receipts are already summed inside it.

options.label: One delivery of goods to an outlet
options.why: Deliveries are movement toward an outlet, not sales out of it, and they live in a different table (fact_sellin, shipments to distributors). Here the column is called revenue and means revenue from a sale to the end customer.

options.label: Stock on hand at an outlet at week's end
options.why: Stock is a point-in-time quantity, and summing it across weeks makes no sense. Here units and revenue are period totals, which sum perfectly normally. Stock lives separately, in fact_stock, and behaves differently.

tasks.title: Plan and actuals in one report
tasks.brief: The requester wants to see plan attainment by SKU: sales and plan side by side. Both tables already exist in the model.
tasks.goal: Work out what such a report will show.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellout — 118,449 rows
  week × outlet × SKU

fact_target — 750 rows
  month × rep × division

Shared dimensions: date only
(and at different granularity)
tasks.predictQuestion: What happens when you try to show plan next to sales, broken down by SKU?
hints: Write out the grain of both tables and find the shared dimensions. There are fewer than you'd think.
What does a product filter do to a table that has no product column at all?
tasks.explain: Measures at different grains coexist in one report only along the dimensions both of them share. Here there's exactly one shared dimension — date, and even that's weekly in one table and monthly in the other. Along any other dimension, the coarser measure behaves the same way every time: it doesn't narrow, and it repeats its full value on every row. The mistake is sneaky because it doesn't look like one — the numbers are there, the report builds, the plan column total just ends up multiplied over. The right answer for the requester here isn't technical, it's substantive: plan by SKU doesn't exist, and before showing it you need to agree on a rule for splitting it.

options.label: Plan won't break down by SKU: it has no product dimension at all. Every report row will repeat the same division plan total
options.why: Plan is recorded by rep and division; product doesn't exist in it in any form. A breakdown by SKU doesn't exist for it, so a product filter doesn't narrow it — every row gets the full plan, regardless of which SKU is selected. And the number looks perfectly normal while doing it.

options.label: The report will refuse to compute: the model won't let you combine tables of different grain
options.why: Nothing refuses. Both tables connect to the calendar, and that's enough to put them side by side. The danger is exactly that the report builds silently and shows a number — just not the one the requester meant.

options.label: Plan will get allocated across SKUs in proportion to sales
options.why: Proportional allocation is separate work that has to be done by hand: setting up a rule for how the division plan splits between products. It doesn't happen on its own, and the model doesn't guess that's what you wanted.

options.label: Plan will come out blank for every row, because there's no product relationship
options.why: It would be blank if the product filter reached fact_target and found nothing there. But this table has no product dimension at all, so there's nothing to filter — instead of blank you get the full total, which is far more dangerous: blank gets noticed right away.

tasks.title: Weeks versus months
tasks.brief: You need to compare shipments to distributors with retail sales: does what left the warehouse match what sold off the shelf.
tasks.goal: Work out at what level of detail this comparison is valid.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellout — shelf sales
  week × outlet × SKU

fact_sellin — warehouse
  shipments: month ×
  distributor × SKU

A week doesn't nest inside a
month cleanly: it can split.
tasks.predictQuestion: At what level can the two measures sit side by side without caveats?
hints: Write both tables' dimensions in two columns and circle the ones present in both.
Which direction does data roll up for free: fine to coarse, or the other way?
tasks.explain: The shared grain of two facts is the intersection of their dimensions, taken at the coarser level of each. Here that's "month × SKU": shipments don't exist below a month, and outlet and distributor belong to different tables. That gives an asymmetric rule worth remembering: aggregating up is always free, splitting down requires introducing an allocation rule — that is, adding your own assumption to the data. That's exactly why sell-in and sell-out comparisons in practice always run monthly and by product: not caution for its own sake, but the only level at which both numbers mean exactly what they are.

options.label: By month and by SKU — the shared part of both grains. Weekly detail isn't available for shipments, and neither is outlet
options.why: The comparison lives at the intersection of the dimensions: SKU is in both tables, date is in both, but the finest shared unit of time is the month. Outlet exists only in sellout, distributor only in sellin, so both of those breakdowns drop out of the joint report.

options.label: By week and by SKU: weekly sales can be summed into a month, and monthly shipments split across weeks proportionally
options.why: The first half is right, the second isn't. You can always sum fine into coarse; splitting coarse into fine takes inventing an allocation rule. Proportional to what? Any answer here is your assumption, not the data, and you'll have to defend it to whoever sees the number.

options.label: By month and by outlet: an outlet unambiguously belongs to its distributor
options.why: The relationship really is unambiguous, but the direction is wrong. A distributor serves many outlets, so its shipment can only be summed upward — to the distributor — and can't be split back down to outlets: fact_sellin simply has no data on how much of a shipment went to each outlet.

options.label: At any level: both tables connect to the calendar, and the report sorts the rest out on its own
options.why: The report builds at any level and shows a number — that's exactly the danger. Along a breakdown missing from one of the tables, that table's measure stops narrowing and repeats in full on every row. Connecting to the calendar is enough to get a number, but not enough for it to mean what you need.

tasks.title: One wide table
tasks.brief: The extract arrives as one table: brand, category, city and region are already sitting right next to sales. The temptation is to leave it as is and build the report straight on top.
tasks.goal: Work out what the biggest cost of that choice turns out to be.
tasks.scenario:
Flat table — 118,449 rows
  week_start, revenue, units,
  product_name, brand,
  category, customer_name,
  city, region_name

Distinct products: 47
Outlets: 144
tasks.predictQuestion: What turns out to be the most expensive cost?
hints: Compare two numbers: how many times a product name is stored, and how many products exist.
What happens if a product gets renamed and some rows get missed in the edit?
tasks.explain: A star schema separates what's measured from what describes it. A measure lives in the fact table, one row per event; an attribute lives in a lookup table, one row per object. The payoff isn't size or speed: it's that every description gets exactly one place to live, and therefore exactly one place to edit. A second consequence is less obvious and shows up sooner than you'd expect: a lookup table exists independently of the fact table, so a product with no sales is still in the report — with its own zero. In a flat table it isn't there at all, and "why is this SKU blank" turns into "did this SKU even exist."

options.label: Consistency: the product name is stored 118,449 times instead of 47, and any edit has to hit every row at once
options.why: Repetition isn't about disk space — it's that the same value exists in thousands of copies and can drift from itself. Miss some rows during a rename, and an extra category shows up in the filter, with the sum split between two spellings of the same brand.

options.label: Size: the table will take up too much space and the model won't fit in memory
options.why: Space is the smallest of the problems here. Low-cardinality columns compress very well — 47 values across 118,449 rows the engine stores efficiently. What bloats a model is high cardinality, not forty-seven repeated names.

options.label: Speed: queries against a wide table are always slower than against a star
options.why: Not always — a flat table has no joins to pay for and can even be faster on simple queries. A flat table's problem isn't performance, and selling a star schema on speed alone means eventually losing a benchmark.

options.label: Nothing significant: as long as data arrives as one extract, there's no reason to split it into a fact and lookups
options.why: "Show all SKUs, including ones that never sold" has no answer on this table at all: a product with no sales simply doesn't exist in it as a row. True right up to the first question that goes beyond what was sold.

tasks.title: Category got split out
tasks.brief: A colleague brought the model "to proper shape": pulled category out of the product lookup into its own table, and from there added a reference to division.
tasks.goal: Work out what this changes in practice.
tasks.scenario:
Before (star):
  fact_sellout → dim_product
  dim_product: brand, category,
               division as columns

After (snowflake):
  fact_sellout → dim_product
  dim_product  → dim_category
  dim_category → dim_division

47 products, 5 categories,
2 divisions.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does this split actually buy here?
hints: Put a number on the win: how many rows does pulling category out of a 47-product lookup actually save?
What happens to the filter's path from a division slicer to the fact table after the split?
tasks.explain: A snowflake is a star with a dimension normalized one step further. It's a legitimate technique, but it has a condition of use: the dimension has to be genuinely large and the repeated attribute has to be heavy. The classic example is a customer lookup with millions of rows and a long region name. Forty-seven products don't qualify, and here splitting just lengthens the filter's path. The general rule for an analytical model runs opposite to what database design trains you to expect: denormalize dimensions until it starts to hurt — a readable model and a short filter path are worth more than the repetition you eliminated.

options.label: Almost nothing: the saving across 47 rows is negligible, and the filter's path to the fact table just got two hops longer
options.why: A snowflake pays off where a dimension is genuinely large and repetition is heavy. Forty-seven products isn't that case: the storage win is indistinguishable, and every extra hop lengthens the filter's path and adds one more place to get a relationship wrong. Here it's pure complexity for nothing.

options.label: The model became more correct: a normalized schema is standard practice for dimensions
options.why: Standard practice for a source, not for an analytical model. Reporting deliberately denormalizes dimensions back, because the priority here is different: read often and heavily, changed rarely and wholesale. Carrying OLTP rules into a model is a common mistake, not a standard to aim for.

options.label: The report will get faster: the engine won't have to read the category column for all 118,449 rows
options.why: It never read it that way to begin with: category lived in a 47-row lookup table, not in the fact table. This is splitting one small lookup table into three even smaller ones — an operation that has zero effect on how fast the fact table reads.

options.label: You gain the ability to filter by division, which wasn't there before
options.why: It was already there: division was a column in the same product lookup and worked as a slicer exactly the same way. Splitting into tables doesn't add breakdowns — it only changes where a value physically lives and how many hops it takes to reach it.

tasks.title: Where to store the price
tasks.brief: The model needs a product's price. It exists in two places: list price in the product lookup, and the actual sale price in the fact row.
tasks.goal: Work out why both columns are needed, and how they differ in meaning.
tasks.scenario:
dim_product.list_price
  list price, one per product

fact_sellout.avg_price
  average sale price
  at this outlet, this week

Sales sometimes include
discounts and promotions.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why can't you keep just list_price from the lookup?
hints: Ask of each column: does it describe an object, or measure an event?
What do you get if you multiply list price by units sold, when half the sales were on promotion?
tasks.explain: The split into fact and dimension isn't about where a column is convenient to sit — it's about what it belongs to. An attribute describes an object and lives in a lookup, one copy. A measure describes an event and lives in the fact table, at its grain. Price falls into both categories because it's two different measures with a similar name: list price is a property of the product, sale price is a property of the transaction. The practical test that tells them apart: if the value can differ between two fact rows with the same product, it belongs to the fact table. Same for everyone — it belongs to the lookup.

options.label: List price describes the product; sale price describes a specific event. Multiply list_price by units and you get revenue with no discounts, not the real thing
options.why: These are different quantities living in different places: one answers "what does the product cost", the other answers "what did it actually sell for, here and then." Discounts and promotions belong to the event, not the product, so the actual price can only be stored at the fact table's grain.

options.label: List price changes over time, and the lookup only holds the current one — that's enough if the model refreshes daily
options.why: A daily refresh doesn't restore the past — it just replaces yesterday's price with today's, and the whole history recomputes under the new one. Tracking an attribute's changes over time is a separate problem (slowly changing dimensions), and it doesn't substitute for the sale price in the fact table.

options.label: For speed: reading price from the fact table is faster than going to fetch it from the lookup
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with it, and it isn't why this decision gets made. Even if the join were free, list_price still wouldn't answer the question about actual revenue — because it's simply a different number, not the same one fetched at a higher cost.

tasks.title: Which way the filter runs
tasks.brief: A report has a brand slicer set. Next to it sit two measures: revenue from the fact table, and a product count from the lookup.
tasks.goal: Work out what the slicer actually affects.
tasks.scenario:
dim_product (47 rows)
  product_id is unique
      │  one-to-many
      ▼
fact_sellout (118,449 rows)

The slicer picks brand «Nettora».
It has 5 products.
tasks.predictQuestion: What will revenue and product count show?
hints: Find the table where the "brand" column physically lives. That's where the filter starts.
By default a filter flows from the "one" side to the "many" side. Which side is which here?
tasks.explain: A relationship in a model isn't a row join — it's a direction filters propagate in. By default there's one: the "one" side filters the "many" side, meaning a lookup narrows a fact table. That's why a star is laid out the way it is: dimensions around the edges, fact in the middle, and any slicer set on a dimension reaches the fact table on its own. The reverse direction is deliberately off — turned on, it creates ambiguity in models with several lookups and noticeably complicates the calculation. A habit that clears up most questions about a number: before you get surprised, trace the path with your finger from the slicer to the table where the measure computes, and check whether it even gets there.

options.label: Both measures narrow to the brand: revenue to its five products, product count to 5. The filter flows from lookup to fact
options.why: The slicer sits on the lookup table, where brand actually lives. The lookup narrows immediately, and along the one-to-many relationship the filter carries on into the fact table, leaving only those five products' rows in the calculation. This direction works by default and needs no extra setup.

options.label: Revenue narrows, but product count stays at 47: the lookup doesn't obey the filter
options.why: It's the other way around: the lookup is the table the slicer is set on directly, and it's the first to narrow. The direction that doesn't obey the filter by default is fact to lookup — but there's no such hop here at all.

options.label: Product count becomes 5, but revenue stays at the full total: the filter from lookup to fact is off by default
options.why: That's exactly the direction that's on by default — the whole mechanics of slicers rests on it. What's off is the reverse: many-to-one. Mixing up these two directions is the most common reason for being surprised by a number on a report.

tasks.title: A relationship on brand
tasks.brief: A colleague wants to link the promo lookup to the product lookup directly by brand — "the field is in both, why not."
tasks.goal: Work out this relationship's cardinality.
tasks.scenario:
dim_product — 47 rows
  distinct brand: 9

dim_promo — 89 rows
  distinct brand: 9

For brand «Nettora»:
  5 products, 10 promos
tasks.predictQuestion: What cardinality results from a relationship on the brand column?
hints: Cardinality is about the key's uniqueness on each side, not about what the word "brand" means.
Compare row count to distinct-brand count in each table. Do they match anywhere at all?
tasks.explain: Cardinality reads mechanically: take the relationship's key and check whether it's unique in the table. Unique on one side — one-to-many. Not unique on either — many-to-many. The singular word "brand" and the phrase "a product has one brand" nudge you toward the wrong answer because they describe meaning, not structure: a product really does have one brand, but in the product table brand repeats forty-seven times across nine values. A many-to-many relationship isn't a ban, it's a warning: you can't join tables like this directly, they need a bridge between them, or every pair inside a group turns into its own row.

options.label: Many-to-many: brand isn't unique in either table — «Nettora»'s five products correspond to its ten promos
options.why: Cardinality is set by the key's uniqueness on each side. Here it's 47 products across 9 brands and 89 promos across 9 brands — repeats on both sides. A relationship like this doesn't match row to row, it matches group to group, and every pair inside a group counts as a match.

options.label: One-to-many: a product has one brand, so the product lookup is the "one" side
options.why: A product really does have one brand, but the "one" side isn't determined by that — it's determined by whether the key is unique in the table. dim_product has 47 rows across 9 brands, meaning the same brand repeats — there's no uniqueness, and this table can't be the "one" side.

options.label: One-to-one: nine brands on one side and nine on the other
options.why: The matching count of distinct values says nothing about cardinality — it's set by row uniqueness, not by how many distinct values exist. One-to-one would hold if brand appeared exactly once in each table, meaning each would have exactly nine rows.

tasks.title: The region slicer has no effect
tasks.brief: A report has shelf sales and warehouse shipments side by side. A region slicer narrows the first and leaves the second untouched.
tasks.goal: Work out why.
tasks.scenario:
dim_region → dim_customer
dim_customer → fact_sellout

fact_sellin.distributor_id
  references dim_customer
  (type distributor only)

12 distributors,
shipping into 16 regions.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why doesn't the region slicer narrow shipments?
hints: Ask what region means in a shipment row: where goods ship from, or where they end up?
There are twelve distributors and sixteen regions. Can a shipment possibly know the destination outlet's region?
tasks.explain: Two role lookups are mixed into one here: dim_customer describes both retail outlets and distributors, and for them region means two different things — where the outlet sits and where the warehouse sits. The filter honestly travels the whole path and honestly narrows shipments, just on a different attribute than the person expected. Cases like this are more dangerous than a missing relationship altogether, because the number changes — so the slicer looks like it's working. The check that catches them: put into words what the dimension means in each table it reaches. Words match — the relationship is correct. Words diverge — you have two different dimensions sharing one name, and at least one of them needs its own name in the report.

options.label: A distributor's own region in the lookup is where the distributor sits, not where the goods end up. A shipment has no idea which region the goods travel on to
options.why: The region filter does reach fact_sellin and does narrow it — but by the distributor's own region, not the region of sale. Twelve distributors deliver goods across sixteen regions, and that link doesn't exist in the shipments table — it only appears one step later, in shelf sales.

options.label: The relationship between dim_customer and fact_sellin isn't set up, so the filter never gets there
options.why: The relationship exists — distributor_id references the same lookup table. If it didn't, shipments wouldn't narrow by any customer breakdown at all, but the question here is different: why the narrowing happens differently than expected.

options.label: The filter direction is set backwards, flowing from the fact table into the lookup
options.why: The reverse direction really is off by default, but it isn't needed here: the path runs from the region lookup, through the customer lookup, into the fact table — the whole way from the "one" side to the "many" side. Direction has nothing to do with it.

options.label: Shipment grain is too coarse: month versus week
options.why: Different date granularity gets in the way of comparing over time, but it has nothing to do with region: if a shipment had a destination region, a slicer on it would work at any time grain. The problem is a missing dimension, not its detail.

tasks.title: Revenue jumped tenfold
tasks.brief: A second path to the promo lookup got added to the model — "to filter sales by the promo's brand." After that, report revenue became ¥1,262,668,596.
tasks.goal: Work out where that number came from.
tasks.scenario:
Path 1 (existing):
  fact_sellout.promo_id
    → dim_promo.promo_id

Path 2 (added):
  fact_sellout.product_id
    → dim_product.brand
      → dim_promo.brand

Total revenue: ¥126,911,191
Now shows: ¥1,262,668,596
Promos per brand: 9-11
tasks.predictQuestion: Where does the tenfold number come from?
hints: Compare the new number not to the old report, but to the table's total revenue. It's bigger than the total.
How many promos will match one sales row if you join on brand?
tasks.explain: A tell worth turning into a reflex: if a measure exceeds the table's full total, it isn't about filters or added rows — something got counted multiple times. Here the second path runs on brand, and brand is non-unique in either the product lookup or the promo lookup. A join on a key like that matches group to group and produces every pair inside it: each brand has 9 to 11 promos, so row count became 1,173,847 instead of 118,449, and revenue became ¥1,262,668,596 instead of ¥126,911,191. Not one row is wrong on its own — the join did exactly what it was asked. The mistake happened earlier, at the moment someone decided the second path was harmless.

options.label: Every sales row matched all of its brand's promos at once — 9 to 11 of them — and that row's revenue got counted just as many times
options.why: A join on a key that's non-unique on both sides multiplies rows by the number of matches. Row count became 1,173,847 instead of 118,449 — almost exactly tenfold — and each one carries the full revenue of its original row. The sum grew by the same factor, because the same value gets summed over and over.

options.label: Non-promo sales made it into the report, ones that were filtered out before
options.why: That would grow the total at most to the full ¥126,911,191 — the entire table's volume, there simply isn't more in it. The resulting number is ten times more than the total revenue there is, so the explanation isn't which rows got added, it's that existing ones got counted repeatedly.

options.label: Double counting: revenue got summed along both the first path and the second
options.why: That would make the result roughly double, and it's ten times bigger. It isn't about the number of paths — it's that the second path runs through a key that's non-unique on either side; the multiplier is the number of promos per brand, not the number of paths.

options.label: A data error: duplicates appeared in the promo lookup
options.why: There are no duplicates there — 89 promos across 9 brands is a normal two-year promo history. The data is fine; the model is wrong: it joins a group of products to a group of promos, when what should be linked is a sales row to its specific promo.

tasks.title: The model refused to choose
tasks.brief: You draw a second relationship between the same two tables. The modeling tool creates it, but marks it dashed and won't let you activate it.
tasks.goal: Work out why this is the response the tool gives.
tasks.scenario:
Between fact_sellout and
dim_promo there are two paths:

  direct — via promo_id
  via dim_product — by brand

The second exists but is
inactive (dashed on the
diagram).
tasks.predictQuestion: Why doesn't the tool activate the second relationship on its own?
hints: Ask how the two paths differ in result. If they gave the same thing, there'd be nothing to choose.
Which is worse: refusing to compute, or a computed number whose meaning nobody can explain?
tasks.explain: An inactive relationship isn't broken — it's deliberately switched off. The model allows the second path to exist but refuses to use it by default, because then every measure would lose a single, unambiguous definition. You can still use a relationship like this, but only explicitly — invoking it inside a specific measure, where the author takes responsibility for the interpretation. Behind this is a principle that separates a model from a query: a query answers one question and lives for a minute; a model answers every future question at once, so ambiguity inside it costs incomparably more. Refusing to compute here isn't a limitation of the tool — it's its best feature.

options.label: Choosing between the paths would change the meaning of every measure, and the tool has no right to guess — it leaves the decision to the model's author
options.why: Two paths give two different answers to one question, and both are formally valid. Choosing on the author's behalf would silently lock one interpretation into every measure in the report. Refusing to compute an ambiguity is noticed right away; a silent choice would show up as a number nobody could explain.

options.label: The second relationship is redundant: it leads to the same rows as the first, just by a longer route
options.why: It doesn't lead to the same rows — that's the whole point. The direct relationship matches a sale to its own promo; the path via brand matches it to all of that brand's promos at once. These are different sets of rows and different numbers, not a long and a short route to the same answer.

options.label: It saves resources: two active relationships between the tables would slow down recalculation
options.why: The restriction exists for unambiguity, not performance. Even if recalculation were free, a model with two active paths couldn't say what its measure means — and that costs more than any slowdown.

options.label: It's a temporary restriction: the relationship will start working after a data refresh
options.why: A data refresh changes nothing — the ambiguity is built into the model's structure, not its content. Dashed doesn't mean "not ready yet" — it's a deliberate state: the relationship exists and can be invoked explicitly from a measure, but doesn't apply by default.

tasks.title: How to keep the two paths apart
tasks.brief: The requester needs both pictures: revenue from the promo a sale actually took part in, and the total revenue of the brand that ran the promo.
tasks.goal: Work out how to satisfy both requests without ambiguity.
tasks.scenario:
Two measures are needed:

  A — revenue via its own promo
  B — revenue of the brand that
      had a promo running

The direct promo_id relationship
is active. The brand
relationship exists but is
inactive.
tasks.predictQuestion: How do you get both measures?
hints: The measures are different, so there should be two of them. The question is what sets the default behaviour.
An inactive relationship isn't useless: you can invoke it from a specific measure without changing the whole model.
tasks.explain: The right answer to ambiguity isn't picking one path forever — it's making the choice explicit and local. The relationship most calculations need stays active and sets the default; the alternative stays inactive and gets switched on inside the one measure that needs it. The payoff is double: the model keeps its unambiguity, and anyone opening the measure list sees two distinctly named measures instead of one with an unresolved meaning. Duplicating the lookup solves the same problem more crudely and costs more to maintain, so it's reached for when explicit invocation is impossible — say, when both interpretations are needed at once inside the same visual.

options.label: Keep the direct relationship active for measure A, and write a separate measure for B that invokes the second relationship explicitly
options.why: The relationship that most measures need stays active — it sets the default behaviour. The second measure gets its own formula, inside which the second path is switched on explicitly, and its name says outright that it computes something different. No ambiguity: every measure has exactly one interpretation.

options.label: Activate both relationships and pick the one you need in each report
options.why: "Choosing in the report" is precisely what a model can't do — that's exactly what explicit invocation inside a measure is for. There's no picking to be done: with two active paths the model doesn't ask which one was meant, it either refuses to create them, or starts computing off one of them silently.

options.label: Delete the promo_id relationship and keep only the brand one: it gives both pictures at once
options.why: It doesn't give either one correctly. A join on brand multiplies rows by the number of promos and overstates revenue roughly tenfold, so measure A can't be built on it at all, and measure B comes out overstated by that exact same factor.

options.label: Add a second copy of the promo lookup to the model and link it by brand
options.why: A copy removes the ambiguity formally — there are no longer two paths to one table — but it moves the problem elsewhere: two lookups with identical content will drift apart at the first refresh, and the field list will show two "promo" tables for a person to guess between. This technique gets used, but as a last resort, not a first one.

tasks.title: Brand share got hard-coded as a number
tasks.brief: Brand «Nettora»'s share of revenue is 12.7% across the whole database. A colleague set it up as a calculated column: computed once and put 12.7% into every fact row.
tasks.goal: Work out what the report shows after a region slicer is applied.
tasks.scenario:
dim_product → fact_sellout
Column: Nettora Share — 12.7%
(written once, into every
fact row)

A slicer for region «Tokyo»
was added to the report.
Correct share for Tokyo: 19.1%
tasks.predictQuestion: What will the column show after the Tokyo slicer?
hints: Remember: a calculated column computes once at refresh, a measure recomputes every time it's displayed.
A slicer changes which rows the report sees. Does it change what's already written into the column?
tasks.explain: A column and a measure look identical in the field list, but behave fundamentally differently under a slicer. A column physically stores a number computed once at data refresh — it knows nothing about future slicers and doesn't recompute for them. A measure doesn't store a number at all: it stores a formula and evaluates it fresh every time the report displays it, accounting for whatever filters are in effect at that moment. The danger is exactly that 12.7% still looks entirely plausible after the slicer — a mistake like this isn't visible to the eye, it only gets caught by checking against an independent calculation.

options.label: Still 12.7% — the slicer doesn't recompute the column, it holds the number that was written into it
options.why: A calculated column computes once at refresh and lives on afterward as ordinary data. A slicer filters which rows the report sees, but it doesn't make the column recompute the value already written into it.

options.label: 19.1% — the column recomputes along with the slicer, like any number on the report
options.why: What recomputes under a slicer is a measure, not a calculated column — that's exactly the difference between them. The column holds the result of one calculation, made at data refresh, before it ever knew about the slicer.

options.label: Blank — the column breaks, because it was computed without accounting for future slicers
options.why: The column doesn't break and doesn't go blank: it holds a perfectly working number, just not the one you need after the slicer. It's a modeling mistake, not a display one — so there's no error message either.

tasks.title: One formula, two ways to set it up
tasks.brief: You're shown two formulas for the same brand share — one set up as a column, the other as a measure. You need to see how they differ in how they compute, not in syntax.
tasks.goal: Work out the difference in when each variant computes.
tasks.predictQuestion: What's the main difference between variant A and variant B in how they compute?
hints: Ignore the difference in DIVIDE's syntax — focus on the difference in when the computation happens.
Ask: when does each of these formulas physically compute — once, or every time it's shown?
tasks.explain: Both formulas look syntactically similar and both use DIVIDE — that's exactly where the confusion comes from. But the context they live in differs: a column is tied to a table row and computes at the moment of data refresh, once and for all, until the next refresh. A measure isn't tied to any row — it exists as a formula and unfolds fresh every time the report asks for its value, taking as input whatever filter context is in effect right now. The number 126911191 hard-coded straight into formula A is an extra red flag: a column can't reach for "the current filtered sum", because at the moment it computes there's no current filter yet.

options.label: A computes once at data refresh and is stored per row; B computes fresh every time it's shown, under the current filter
options.why: That's exactly the defining difference between a column and a measure — it isn't about DIVIDE's syntax, it's about when the computation happens. A column has one such moment, at data refresh; a measure has one every time it's displayed.

options.label: A runs faster, because it contains the number 126911191 directly instead of referencing another measure
options.why: The number inside formula A has nothing to do with how fast it runs. Speed isn't the main difference here at all — the main difference is when the formula computes: once at refresh, or fresh every time it's shown.

options.label: A and B give the same result in any report; the difference is purely cosmetic
options.why: The results only match in one special case — a report with no slicers at all. Add any filter by region or brand, and A keeps showing the number computed at refresh, while B recomputes.

tasks.title: A column for every slicer combination
tasks.brief: A colleague proposes a compromise: since a measure recomputes slower than a column, set up a separate column for every slicer you need — by region, by brand, by region and brand together.
tasks.goal: Work out what's wrong with this plan, beyond the growing number of columns.
tasks.scenario:
Proposed:

  ShareByRegion (column)
  ShareByBrand (column)
  ShareByRegionBrand (column)

Each for every slicer
combination known so far.
tasks.predictQuestion: What happens to this plan at the first unplanned slicer?
hints: Put a number on it: how many possible slicer combinations exist (region, brand, month, channel...) versus how many columns you could realistically pre-build?
A measure answers any slicer with one formula. How many formulas do columns need to do the same?
tasks.explain: The idea of "a column for every slicer" doesn't break on the first case or the second — it breaks on the third, the slicer nobody foresaw. A measure solves this fundamentally differently: it doesn't enumerate combinations of conditions in advance, it computes under whatever filter context happens to form in a given report cell, whatever that turns out to be. One formula answers any conceivable slicer, because it doesn't store the answer — it stores how to get it. That's exactly why measures are the standard way to compute quantities that need to behave correctly under a slicer, while calculated columns get left for things that genuinely don't change with a slicer: a category, a status, a flag.

options.label: For a slicer nobody set up a column for in advance, there will be no correct number at all — the columns only cover the combinations that were planned
options.why: A column computes once for a specific, known-in-advance combination of conditions. The moment the requester asks for a slicer by month or by sales channel that no column was set up for, there's nothing to answer with — a column for that case simply doesn't exist.

options.label: Nothing serious: there'll be more columns, but each keeps showing the correct number for its own combination
options.why: True for combinations already planned for, but the plan is fragile at exactly the moment a combination shows up that wasn't foreseen. And foreseeing every possible slicer a report might ever need is impossible in principle — there are too many combinations.

options.label: The model will refuse to create the third column, because combining two dimensions isn't supported in DAX
options.why: There's no technical limit on a formula like this — DIVIDE with two filter conditions writes freely. The problem isn't that the column can't be created — it's that the whole approach doesn't scale to slicers nobody planned for.

tasks.title: What a cell's filter is made of
tasks.brief: In a matrix report, a cell sits at the intersection of row «Tokyo» and a page-level slicer for «Nettora». The measure is Revenue.
tasks.goal: Work out what makes up this cell's filter context.
tasks.scenario:
Matrix:
  row = region («Tokyo»)
  page slicer = brand «Nettora»

Measure: Revenue = SUM(revenue)
Revenue in the cell: ¥819,771
tasks.predictQuestion: Which of the following is part of this cell's filter context?
hints: Mentally remove one of the two sources — the slicer or the row — and ask whether the number in the cell changes.
A matrix row works the same way as a row in GROUP BY: it doesn't just label, it also restricts.
tasks.explain: A report cell isn't one condition — it's the intersection of every condition currently acting on it. Here there are two: the row sets the region, the page slicer sets the brand, and the measure sees both at once, as if joined with AND. Remove either source and the number in the cell changes — that's the practical test: remove the slicer and keep the row, and you get all of Tokyo's revenue across every brand, ¥3,718,723 instead of ¥819,771. The habit of listing filter sources one at a time — row, column, slicers, filters baked into the measure itself — saves more time than any other report-reading skill.

options.label: Both the row's condition (region = «Tokyo») and the page slicer's condition (brand = «Nettora») — both apply at once
options.why: A cell's filter context is made up of every source at once, not just one. A matrix row and a page slicer are two independent sources, and both narrow the data down to what meets both conditions.

options.label: Only the row's condition — page slicers don't affect individual matrix cells
options.why: A page slicer applies to the whole page, including every cell of every matrix on it — that's exactly what it's for. If the slicer didn't reach the cells, the number in them wouldn't change when a brand is picked, but it does: without the slicer it would be ¥3,718,723.

options.label: Only the slicer's condition — a matrix row sets a label, not a filter
options.why: A matrix row isn't just a label: every row by region physically filters the data down to that region, otherwise the «Tokyo» and «Osaka» rows would show the same number. Here, labeling and filtering are one and the same action.

tasks.title: A measure with its own filter inside
tasks.brief: The "Nettora Revenue" measure already has a brand condition baked into its formula. It gets put into a by-region matrix with no slicer on the page at all.
tasks.goal: Work out what the "Tokyo" cell shows.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does the "Tokyo" row show, if there's no brand slicer on the page at all?
hints: The brand condition sits inside CALCULATE, not outside the measure. Does it need an external slicer to fire?
Compare with mdl-019: there the condition came from a page slicer. Where does it come from here?
tasks.explain: A cell's filter context isn't made up only of rows, columns and page slicers — there's a fourth source: conditions baked into the measure itself via CALCULATE. A filter like this doesn't depend on what's selected outside it: it applies every time the measure is invoked, whether there's a brand slicer on the page or not. The practical takeaway: two measures shown side by side on a report ("Revenue" and "Nettora Revenue") can behave differently under the exact same set of external slicers — and understanding why takes more than looking at the report page, you have to look inside the measure's own formula.

options.label: ¥1,691,942 — Nettora's revenue for Tokyo. The brand filter always applies, because it's part of the measure itself, not an external slicer
options.why: The condition dim_product[brand]="Nettora" is baked inside CALCULATE and acts as a fourth source of filter context — the measure's own filter. It doesn't need a page slicer: it applies every time the measure is invoked, regardless of what's selected outside it.

options.label: ¥8,876,489 — Tokyo's full revenue across every brand, because there's no brand slicer on the page
options.why: That would be true for a measure with no internal filter, like a plain Revenue. But Nettora Revenue has the brand condition built into its formula, and it doesn't depend on whether there's a page slicer — it's always there.

options.label: Blank — without an external brand slicer, CALCULATE can't evaluate the condition inside it
options.why: CALCULATE exists precisely to set filter conditions explicitly, without external slicers. The formula here is complete and working — it evaluates its own condition; the filter's source is simply different, the measure itself rather than a page slicer.

tasks.title: The "Total" row at the bottom
tasks.brief: The same by-region matrix has a "Total" row underneath it. A slicer for brand «Nettora» is set on the page.
tasks.goal: Work out what filter context applies in the "Total" row.
tasks.scenario:
Matrix with a «Nettora» slicer:

  Tokyo      1,691,942
  Saitama    2,441,558
  ...
  Total     16,165,815
tasks.predictQuestion: What filter context applies in the "Total" row?
hints: Ask: does a region value "Total" exist in the dim_region lookup? If not, what is this row's filter resting on?
Compare the "Total" row to the "Tokyo" row by the number of filter sources, not by the final figure.
tasks.explain: "Total" isn't a sum of the displayed rows computed separately by the visual — it's the same measure invoked under its own filter context, one condition lighter. An ordinary row combines the page slicer with a condition on its own region; the "Total" row sees only the page slicer, with no region condition at all. This explains behavior that would otherwise look strange: "Total" recomputes on its own when new regions are added to the lookup, because it doesn't store a list of what to add up — it simply computes in a context with fewer restrictions.

options.label: Only the page slicer (brand = «Nettora») — with no region condition, because the "Total" row isn't tied to any specific region
options.why: "Total" isn't another region — it's a row with no region condition of its own: only the page slicer remains in its filter context. That's why it shows the sum across every region at once — the same figure a brand slicer alone would give, with no row breakdown at all.

options.label: Region = all sixteen at once, joined with OR — the same as an ordinary row, just with the full list
options.why: Formally that would give the same result, but in fact the "Total" row isn't built as a list of region conditions — it's built as the absence of any region condition at all. The difference is practical: add a seventeenth region to the lookup, and the "Total" row picks it up on its own, while an "all sixteen joined with OR" list would need rewriting.

options.label: The same filter context as the "Tokyo" row, plus an extra condition "region = Total"
options.why: "Total" is an element of the visual, not a lookup value — no such region value exists in any table in the model. A row can't have a condition on a value that doesn't exist; it's more accurate to say the row simply has no region condition at all.

tasks.title: SUM inside a row-level column
tasks.brief: A new calculated column gets added to fact_sellout, to look at each individual sale's revenue right next to the row.
tasks.goal: Work out what the column shows in the table's first row.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does this column show in the first row?
hints: SUM is an aggregating function. It responds to filter context, not row context.
How many rows does the filter restrict at the moment this new column computes, if no slicer has been applied yet?
tasks.explain: This is the most common trap with calculated columns: row context gives the formula access to the current row's values, but it doesn't force aggregating functions like SUM to use that row specifically. SUM only responds to the filter context, and at the moment an ordinary column computes, that context is simply empty — nothing is filtered. So SUM(fact_sellout[revenue]) sums revenue across the entire table and puts the same number, 126,911,191, into every single row without exception. To get the current row's own value, an aggregating function isn't needed at all — a direct reference to the column is enough.

options.label: 126,911,191 — the sum of revenue across the whole table. SUM ignores row context and aggregates whatever isn't filtered, and here nothing is filtered
options.why: SUM is an aggregating function — it responds to the filter context, not the row context. At the moment the column computes, no filter is in effect, so SUM adds up every row in the table — and gets the same result in every row.

options.label: 398.31 — this row's own revenue value, because the column computes in row context
options.why: That's how a plain reference to the column would work — "=fact_sellout[revenue]" with no SUM. But SUM inside the formula changes things: aggregating functions don't read row context directly, they aggregate over the filter context, which here is empty and restricts nothing.

options.label: A calculation error — SUM can't be used inside a calculated column
options.why: The formula is syntactically fine, there's no error. SUM inside a calculated column is entirely legal — it's just that the result is almost never what people expect: it equals the sum across the whole table, not the current row.

tasks.title: The fix without aggregation
tasks.brief: You still need revenue per unit for each row — not the table's overall total, but exactly that row's own value.
tasks.goal: Work out which formula solves this correctly.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which variant returns the first row's own price, 199.16, for that row?
hints: Compare the two variants on one point: is there a SUM or a similar aggregating function inside either of them?
Row context works on its own for direct column references — an aggregating function overrides it.
tasks.explain: The difference between the two variants isn't DIVIDE — it's identical in both formulas and just divides two numbers. The difference is what's inside DIVIDE. In variant A those are direct references to the current row's columns: revenue and units are pulled from that row specifically, and row context works with no extra effort. In variant B there's a SUM inside — and SUM, just as in the previous task, responds not to the row but to the filter context, which is absent here, and aggregates the entire table. The practical takeaway: if a column formula needs to answer "for this row", aggregating functions mostly have no place in it — only direct field references do.

options.label: Variant A — direct references to revenue and units, with no aggregating functions, naturally use row context
options.why: DIVIDE here just divides two values, and the values themselves are direct references to the current row's columns. Nothing stops row context from doing its job: for the first row that's 398.31 and 2, giving 199.16 — that specific sale's own price.

options.label: Variant B — SUM inside DIVIDE sums exactly the row the formula is applied to
options.why: SUM behaves the same regardless of what wraps around it — it still responds to filter context, not row context. Variant B returns the same number in every row: the overall price per unit across the whole table.

options.label: Both variants give the same result — DIVIDE normalizes the difference between them
options.why: DIVIDE is an ordinary division function — it doesn't change how its arguments compute. If one argument is aggregated across the whole table and the other isn't, DIVIDE can't magically reconcile them into the same context.

tasks.title: Row context inside an iterator
tasks.brief: Unlike an ordinary column, a formula inside SUMX or a similar iterator function runs separately for each row — and there SUM behaves differently.
tasks.goal: Work out why the same SUM inside an iterator no longer gives the table-wide total.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why does revenue inside SUMX here behave like the current row's value, rather than the table's total?
hints: SUMX isn't an ordinary aggregating function like SUM — it's an iterator: it walks rows one at a time.
Ask: who creates row context in this example — a calculated column (like mdl-022), or SUMX itself?
tasks.explain: In the previous two tasks, row context already existed — a calculated column supplied it, and SUM inside it ignored that context, because SUM only responds to filter context. Here the source is different: SUMX itself creates row context by walking fact_sellout row by row, and for each row it evaluates the expression passed to it inside that exact context — only afterward summing the results across every row. That's why inside SUMX a direct column reference means the current iteration row's value, not the table's total. This is the key difference between iterator functions (SUMX, AVERAGEX, FILTER) and ordinary aggregating functions: they don't just aggregate — they iterate, and at every step of the iteration the formula inside has its own row context, one the function itself built.

options.label: SUMX itself creates a row context for every row of fact_sellout and evaluates the expression passed to it inside that context — before summing the results at the end
options.why: SUMX is an iterator function: it walks the table row by row and creates its own row context for each row, and that's the context the expression passed to it computes in. Inside that context, a direct reference to fact_sellout[revenue] means "this row's own revenue value", not the table's total.

options.label: SUM inside SUMX always refers to the current row — a special exception to the general rule about SUM
options.why: There's no separate SUM function inside the expression at all — just direct column references multiplied and divided against each other. The rule about SUM (responds to filter context, ignores row context) doesn't change; what changes is that SUMX itself supplies a row context that wouldn't exist in an ordinary column.

options.label: The formula is flawed: units*revenue/units always equals revenue, and you can't write it this redundantly
options.why: The formula really does reduce to revenue mathematically — but the question isn't about writing it efficiently, it's about the computation mechanism. Even written redundantly, it demonstrates exactly how SUMX creates a row-by-row context, which is the whole point of the task.

tasks.title: Three measures, three ways to sum
tasks.brief: The model has three measures: revenue, stock on hand, and average sale price. You need to decide which breakdowns each can be summed across without distorting its meaning.
tasks.goal: Work out each of the three measures' additivity.
tasks.scenario:
Three measures:

  Revenue — ¥
  StockOnHand — units
  AvgPrice — average price, ¥

Stock is counted at the end
of each month (a snapshot).
tasks.predictQuestion: Which of the three measures can be summed across ANY breakdown, including time?
hints: Ask of each measure: does it accumulate over a period (like money in a till), or exist at every moment (like stock on a shelf)?
An additive measure sums across time exactly as honestly as across any other breakdown — no exceptions.
tasks.explain: The three measures represent three classes of additivity, and the line between them isn't drawn by the unit of measurement but by what happens to the meaning when you sum. Revenue is additive: it belongs to a sale event, and events can be summed along any dimension, time included. Stock on hand is semi-additive: it belongs to a point in time, not a period, so it sums across everything that isn't time (product, region, distributor) but not across time itself. Average price isn't additive at all: it's already the result of a division, and summing several such results doesn't mean anything — it needs to be recomputed fresh at whatever level you need, not summed from ready-made averages.

options.label: Only Revenue — revenue accumulates over a period and sums equally honestly by product, region and month
options.why: Revenue is a classic additive quantity: every unit of it belongs to a specific sale, and a sum across any set of sales means exactly what it should — total revenue for that set, regardless of whether you slice it by product, region or time.

options.label: Only StockOnHand — stock on hand physically exists at every moment, so it can be summed across any period
options.why: Physically existing at every moment is exactly why stock CAN'T be summed across time: adding up several snapshots of the same inventory doesn't mean anything meaningful. Summed across products and regions at the same point in time, stock works fine — that's the "semi" in semi-additive.

options.label: Only AvgPrice — average price is the same across any breakdown, so summing it isn't distorted
options.why: Average price is the opposite of "the same across any breakdown": it's usually different for every product, region and period. Adding up several different average prices and getting a meaningful number is impossible along any breakdown at all — it's a non-additive quantity.

tasks.title: Quarterly stock as one sum
tasks.brief: The requester wants one number — "the distributor's stock on hand for Q4." The model has stock computed at the end of every month.
tasks.goal: Work out what SUM across the quarter's three months shows.
tasks.scenario:
Distributor stock, all
products, month end:

  October    10,325 units
  November   15,108 units
  December   20,846 units

SUM for the quarter = 46,279
tasks.predictQuestion: What does 46,279 mean, and is it a valid answer for the requester?
hints: Ask: what does 46,279 units physically mean? Did that much stock ever sit in the warehouse at once?
"Stock for a period" almost always means stock AT THE END of the period, not a sum of the stock levels inside it.
tasks.explain: The mistake looks innocent, because SUM is exactly the function that works for revenue and units sold. For stock it works differently: stock is a snapshot of state at a moment, not the accumulation of an event, and three snapshots of the same physical inventory don't add up to a new physical meaning. The right answer to "stock for the quarter" is the value at quarter end, December's 20,846 units, because that's what answers "how much stock is sitting in the warehouse right now, at the end of the period." In DAX this is expressed via LASTDATE or CALCULATE with a filter on the period's last day, not a plain SUM — but the idea matters more than the syntax: first work out what operation the quantity's meaning calls for, only then write the formula.

options.label: Not valid: it's the sum of three separate point-in-time snapshots of the same inventory — no such stock level ever existed at any single moment
options.why: Stock on hand isn't something that accumulates over a month — it's something that exists at a specific moment, usually period end. Adding up three snapshots of goods that partly sat in the warehouse across all three months counts the same physical goods more than once.

options.label: Valid: it's the distributor's total stock for the quarter, exactly what the requester asked for
options.why: The requester asked about stock "for the quarter", but the meaningful answer to that isn't a sum of monthly snapshots — it's the value at quarter end, meaning December's 20,846 units. "For the quarter" here means the moment the period ends, not accumulation inside it.

options.label: Valid, but the result needs dividing by three to get the average stock
options.why: Dividing by three gives the average monthly stock — a metric in its own right, sometimes useful, but not what people usually mean by "stock on hand for the quarter." The answer to the original question is the ending stock at the cutoff date, December's 20,846, not an average of three snapshots.

tasks.title: Annual stock came out sevenfold off
tasks.brief: A dashboard showed stock on hand for 2025 as 370,142 units. The actual stock at the end of December, checked physically against the warehouse, is 52,350 units.
tasks.goal: Work out what's causing the discrepancy, and how to fix it.
tasks.scenario:
Dashboard: SUM(units_on_hand)
across all 12 months of 2025
= 370,142 units

Actual warehouse stock at
end of December 2025: 52,350

Discrepancy — almost sevenfold.
tasks.predictQuestion: What's causing the discrepancy, and how do you fix it?
hints: Compare 370,142 to the sum of the distributor's twelve monthly stock figures — does it come close?
Remember mdl-026: the same effect showed up across a quarter's three months, here it's across a year's twelve.
tasks.explain: The mistake at annual scale is the same as the quarterly one in mdl-026, just more visible: summing twelve snapshots of growing stock gives a total several times larger than any of the values it's built from, because every snapshot partly re-counts the same physical goods that sat in the warehouse for more than one month. A measure meant to answer "stock at year end" has to take the value on the year's last date, not sum the intermediate snapshots. The practical lesson goes wider than this one case: any measure built over a semi-additive quantity needs a separate formula for every time breakdown — annual, quarterly and monthly versions of stock don't reduce to each other by simple summing, unlike revenue, where the annual measure is exactly the sum of the monthly ones.

options.label: The measure sums 12 monthly stock snapshots instead of taking the snapshot at year end. The fix is to replace SUM with the value at the end of the period
options.why: This is the same semi-additive effect, just at annual scale: stock at the end of each of the 12 months was, on average, growing, and summing every snapshot recounts the same physically-sitting goods over and over. The right way to get "stock for the year" is to take the snapshot on the period's last date, not the sum of the months inside it.

options.label: The fact_stock rows are duplicated in the data, and some stock got counted twice
options.why: Row duplication would give exactly a twofold discrepancy in the affected months, not a steady climb across all twelve. A sevenfold discrepancy and its cumulative shape point to the arithmetic of summing snapshots over time, not a data defect.

options.label: The dashboard is computing off the wrong distributor — check the distributor_id filter
options.why: A wrong distributor filter would give a different number, but not necessarily one that's a clean multiple bigger — just a different warehouse's stock. Here the tell points elsewhere: the total is roughly the sum of the climbing monthly stock levels, which points straight at semi-additivity, not a mixed-up filter.

tasks.title: Without a shared calendar
tasks.brief: The model doesn't have a separate date table yet. A quarter slicer got built straight on the week_start column in fact_sellout — it only exists there.
tasks.goal: Work out what happens to fact_sellin with a slicer like this.
tasks.scenario:
The slicer is built on:
  fact_sellout.week_start

There's no separate relationship
