with fact_sellin — it has its
own month_start column, and
it isn't linked to the
week_start slicer.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does the shipment measure (fact_sellin) show with this slicer?
hints: Ask what region means in a shipment row: where goods ship from, or where they end up?
There's no relationship between the two fact tables' date columns — trace whether a filter has any path at all between them.
tasks.explain: Without a shared date table, every fact table is on its own: a slicer built on its own date column filters only that table and whatever is directly connected to it. fact_sellout and fact_sellin have no relationship between them here at all — different columns, different names, different granularity, week_start versus month_start — and a filter placed on one has no path at all to the other. The result is worse than an outright error: the report silently shows a shipments number that ignores the slicer, and it's easy to mistake for correct, because nothing visually signals a problem.

options.label: The full total, ignoring the slicer — a slicer built on one fact table's column doesn't affect another fact table that has no relationship to that column
options.why: A slicer filters the table its column is built on, and everything connected to it. fact_sellin has no relationship whatsoever to fact_sellout's week_start — it has its own date column, and without a shared date table there's no path between the two facts a filter could travel along.

options.label: The same total as sales — both fact tables are, in the end, about the same product and period
options.why: A shared topic (sales and shipments of the same product) doesn't create a relationship in the model automatically. A model filters along explicitly defined relationships between tables, not by how semantically close the data is — and there's currently no relationship between these two columns.

options.label: An error — DAX won't let you build a slicer on a column that isn't connected to other tables
options.why: Building a slicer on a column like this is entirely allowed, there's no error. The problem is quieter and more dangerous than an error: the slicer simply won't apply where there's no relationship, and the number on the report ends up wrong with no warning at all.

tasks.title: One calendar row serving both
tasks.brief: dim_date got added to the model. A specific day, March 3rd 2025, is picked, and its row is examined.
tasks.goal: Work out how one calendar row connects a weekly fact table and a monthly one.
tasks.scenario:
dim_date, row for 2025-03-03:

  date_id     2025-03-03
  week_start  2025-03-03
  month_start 2025-03-01
  quarter     1

fact_sellout.week_start
holds 2025-03-03.
fact_sellin.month_start
holds 2025-03-01,
but NOT 2025-03-03.
tasks.predictQuestion: How does this one dim_date row connect both facts, if their date values differ?
hints: Look at the dim_date row for March 3rd again: how many different dates does it hold, and which fact table needs which?
What's shared in this row isn't a specific date value — it's the year and quarter this row belongs to.
tasks.explain: The trick of a date table is that it's stored by day — the finest unit — but carries derived columns for every coarser grouping: week, month, quarter, year. The March 3rd row is simultaneously "the start of its own week" (for fact_sellout), "belongs to March, which starts on the 1st" (for fact_sellin), and "Q1" — all at once, in the same fields of the same row. Each fact table builds a relationship to the dim_date column it actually needs, not to the other fact's column: the weekly fact to week_start, the monthly fact to month_start. Both paths ultimately converge on the shared year and quarter, which is why a quarter slicer on dim_date filters both facts at once, even though their own native date values never coincide.

options.label: Through two separate relationships to the same table: date_id to week_start for one fact, and date_id to month_start for the other — both paths lead into one calendar
options.why: dim_date is stored by day, and it has separate columns for different granularities — its own week_start and its own month_start, in the same row. Each fact table connects to its own dim_date column, and both relationships ultimately lead to the same calendar, with shared year and quarter.

options.label: It can't: since the date values are literally different (2025-03-03 and 2025-03-01), there can be no shared slicer for the two facts
options.why: The values really are literally different, but dim_date doesn't require a literal match between the two facts directly — it's an intermediary with a separate column for each granularity. That's exactly why one and the same quarter on dim_date filters both facts, even though their own dates never coincide.

options.label: By converting month_start in fact_sellin to a weekly format before building the relationship
options.why: No conversion is needed at all — dim_date already holds both required granularities in the same table, just in different columns of the same row. The task is solved with relationships to existing columns, not by transforming the fact table's data.

tasks.title: One slicer, both reports line up
tasks.brief: The dashboard has weekly sales and monthly shipments side by side, both connected to dim_date. The requester sets a slicer "quarter = 1, year = 2025."
tasks.goal: Work out whether the two reports show consistent numbers, and why.
tasks.scenario:
Slicer: year=2025, quarter=1

Sales (weekly,
via dim_date.week_start):
  ¥13,512,252

Shipments (monthly,
via dim_date.month_start):
  ¥9,186,879
tasks.predictQuestion: Different numbers — is this a broken relationship or an expected result?
hints: Ask yourself: what should a shared calendar actually guarantee — matching numbers, or a matching time window?
Sell-in and sell-out are two different flows: from a distributor's warehouse, and off a retail shelf. Should they physically match?
tasks.explain: A shared date table solves one specific problem — it guarantees that a "Q1, 2025" slicer means the same window of time for every fact table connected to it, regardless of their native granularity. It doesn't solve, and doesn't promise to solve, a different problem — making different business measures equal to each other. Shelf sales and shipments to distributors are independent processes with their own dynamics: a warehouse stocks up ahead of time, retail sells gradually, and over any given quarter these two flows will almost never match in money. The value of a shared calendar is precisely that it makes a comparison like this possible and honest in the first place: both figures answer the question about the same period, and the gap between them can now be analyzed on its merits — instead of wondering whether the period boundaries themselves drifted apart.

options.label: Expected: both figures are honestly computed over the same quarter, through one calendar, and the gap between them is the gap between shelf sales and warehouse shipments — not a relationship bug
options.why: A shared calendar guarantees both reports answer the question "what happened in Q1 2025" — and that's the only thing it guarantees. It doesn't promise that sell-in and sell-out will turn out equal: these are different business processes (retail sales and warehouse replenishment), and it's natural to expect their totals over the same period to diverge.

options.label: A relationship bug: if the calendar is shared, both reports have to show the same number for one period
options.why: A shared calendar ties both facts to the same time window — but it doesn't turn different quantities into one. Shelf sales and warehouse shipments measure fundamentally different events, and their being equal would be a suspicious coincidence rather than the norm.

options.label: A relationship bug: fact_sellin should filter through week_start, not month_start, and the numbers would match
options.why: fact_sellin has no week_start column at all — only monthly granularity, shipments aren't detailed by week in this model. Even if that relationship existed technically, sales and shipments would still be different processes with different totals, because they measure two different things.

tasks.title: March revenue — by which date
tasks.brief: The requester asks for March 2025 shipment revenue. The table has two dates: when it was ordered and when it shipped. They didn't specify which, and you didn't ask.
tasks.goal: Work out why two calculations give different numbers, and both are correct.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellin, March 2025:

  by order date    ¥3,303,414
  by ship date     ¥3,570,458

Shipping lags ordering by
2-11 days. Of 15,362 orders,
1,979 ship the following month.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why do the numbers diverge, and which one is correct?
hints: Look at the 1,979 orders whose order month and ship month differ. Where do they land in each of the two calculations?
Ask what question each figure answers before picking the "correct" one.
tasks.explain: Two dates in one fact table aren't redundancy — they're two different events in one row's life. "Revenue for March" without a date specified is an incomplete question, and the right analyst response isn't to choose for the requester, it's to send the clarification back: do we count by the moment of the deal, or the moment of shipping? In the model this is set up as one date table with two relationships to it: the active one sets the default behaviour, the second stays inactive and gets switched on explicitly inside whichever measure needs it. Across all of 2025 the gap nearly vanishes (¥39,104,808 against ¥39,023,501) — over a long enough horizon the boundary effect averages out, which is exactly why it shows up on monthly reports and not on annual ones.

options.label: Both are correct — they answer different questions. Late-February orders shipped in March, and late-March orders will ship in April
options.why: Neither figure is wrong: one answers "how much was ordered in March", the other "how much shipped in March." The ¥267,000 gap is the pure effect of the month boundary, which 1,979 of the 15,362 orders cross.

options.label: The order-date figure is correct: the order is the moment of the deal, shipping is just its fulfillment
options.why: That might be right for a sales report, but not for a logistics or warehouse report: there, what matters is when the goods physically left. Which date is "correct" is set by the requester's question, not by any property of the dates themselves.

options.label: The difference means lost orders: ¥267,000 was ordered but never shipped
options.why: Nothing is lost — late-March orders simply ship in April and land in April's figure. The balance reconciles over a long enough horizon: across all of 2025, orders total ¥39,104,808, shipments ¥39,023,501, and the difference is just the tail at year end.

options.label: This is a modeling error: two dates can't connect to one calendar, you need two date tables
options.why: Two date tables would actually be the mistake — the field list would end up with two "Year" columns and two slicers to guess between. One date playing two roles gets solved with an active and an inactive relationship to a single calendar.

tasks.title: Two relationships to one calendar
tasks.brief: You're connecting fact_sellin to dim_date. The first relationship, on order_date, is created active. The second, on ship_date, the tool creates dashed.
tasks.goal: Work out why the second relationship is inactive, and what that changes.
tasks.scenario:

  (solid, active)

dim_date ← fact_sellin.ship_date
  (dashed, inactive)

Page slicer: March 2025.

tasks.predictQuestion: What does a plain Revenue measure compute with a "March 2025" slicer?
hints: A dashed relationship exists in the model but doesn't carry the filter. How many paths does the filter from the calendar have left?
Compare with mdl-014: the dashed line showed up there for the same reason — to give the filter a single path.
tasks.explain: An inactive relationship is a way to have a second path in the model without creating ambiguity. By default the filter travels only along the active one, and every measure computes the same way — by order date. A measure that needs the calendar's second role switches it on locally: CALCULATE(SUM(net_amount), USERELATIONSHIP(fact_sellin[ship_date], dim_date[date_id])). A measure like this gets its own name, something like "Revenue by shipment", and a person opening the field list sees two distinctly named measures instead of one with an unresolved meaning. It's the same principle as in mdl-015: the choice between interpretations is made explicit and local, not by flipping a switch on the whole model.

options.label: ¥3,303,414 — by order date, because the filter only travels along the active relationship. The inactive one plays no part until it's switched on explicitly
options.why: The active relationship sets the default behaviour: the filter from the calendar travels along it and no other. The inactive one exists in the model but doesn't carry the filter — it's waiting for a specific measure to invoke it via USERELATIONSHIP.

options.label: ¥3,570,458 — by ship date, because ship_date is later and the model uses the more recent date
options.why: The model doesn't pick the "more recent" date — it has no such concept. The choice is made by the author, by marking one relationship active; everything else follows from that.

options.label: The sum of both figures, because the March filter travels along both relationships
options.why: If both relationships were active at once, the model simply wouldn't let you create them — that would be the ambiguity from mdl-014. That's exactly why the second one is marked inactive: to keep the filter's path singular.

options.label: An ambiguity error: two relationships between the same pair of tables aren't allowed
options.why: Two relationships between one pair of tables are allowed precisely on the condition that only one of them is active. The error would occur if you tried to make both active — that's exactly what the dashed line prevents.

tasks.title: A second calendar instead of a second relationship
tasks.brief: A colleague proposes doing without inactive relationships: add a second date table to the model — dim_ship_date — and connect it directly to ship_date.
tasks.goal: Work out the main consequence of this choice for whoever opens the report.

Proposed:

  dim_ship_date → ship_date

year, quarter, month columns.
tasks.predictQuestion: What happens when someone puts a year slicer on the page?

Someone sets a year and sees two numbers side by side, one for the chosen period and the other for the entire history. The general rule: one time axis, one calendar, however many dates sit in the fact tables. Separate calendars only get set up when the axes are genuinely different — a separate fiscal year with a shifted start, say, that its own reporting is built on. A date's role within one axis is a relationships question, not a new-tables question.

Two numbers for different periods end up sitting side by side, and there's nothing about it that visually looks different from a normal report.

options.label: Both measures narrow correctly: the calendars contain the same dates, so a year slicer works the same way on both
options.why: Identical content doesn't create a relationship. A filter propagates along the model's relationships, and a slicer on dim_date is connected only to order_date — there's no path at all to ship_date, however many identical dates sit in the second table.

options.label: The model will refuse to work: two calendars in one model aren't allowed
options.why: Two calendars are technically allowed and sometimes even needed — different fiscal years, for instance. The problem isn't a ban — it's that here the second calendar describes the exact same time axis, and its existence only misleads people.

options.label: The report will get twice as slow, because the model will recompute both calendars
options.why: A 912-row calendar isn't going to slow anything down noticeably — it's one of the smallest tables in the model. The cost of this choice isn't speed — it's that the report starts silently showing incomparable numbers side by side.

tasks.title: The key isn't unique anywhere
tasks.brief: You need to link the product lookup to the promo lookup, to filter sales by a promo's brand. There's a shared column — brand.
tasks.goal: Work out the cardinality, and what to do about it.

dim_promo — 89 rows
  distinct brand: 9

Brand «Nettora»:

tasks.predictQuestion: What does a direct relationship on brand give you, and what's the right way to link these?

Matches in at least one — an ordinary one-to-many relationship. Matches in neither — many-to-many, and it can't be built directly. A bridge solves this by pulling the pairs out into a separate table: 465 unique "product × promo" combinations across all nine brands, to which both dim_product and dim_promo connect the way lookups connect to a fact table. options.why: The key repeats on both sides — 47 rows across 9 brands, and 89 across the same 9. A direct relationship matches group to group: «Nettora»'s five products would each produce ten pairs — fifty rows instead of five. A bridge fixes these pairs explicitly, and both relationships to it become one-to-many.

options.label: One-to-many: a product has one brand, so dim_product will be the "one" side
options.why: The "one" side is determined by the key's uniqueness in the table, not by how many brands one product has. In dim_product, brand repeats — 47 rows across 9 values — so there's no uniqueness, and this table can't be the "one" side.

options.label: No relationship is needed at all: fact_sellout is already connected to dim_promo via promo_id
options.why: promo_id answers a different question — "which promo did this specific sale take part in." The question here is different: which products even belong to the brand that had a promo. This is a relationship between two lookup tables, and promo_id doesn't answer it.

tasks.title: How many rows are in the bridge

«Nettora»: 5 products, 10 promos
