hints: Within a brand, every product pairs with every promo. What operation is that?
Check it against «Nettora»: 5 products and 10 promos. How many pairs?
tasks.explain: A bridge is a materialized list of valid combinations, one row per pair. Its size is the sum of the products within each group: nine brands, each with its own products and its own promos, and each one's contribution is the product of those two counts. That gives 465 rows out of 47 products and 89 promos. It matters that the bridge is bigger than both source tables — that's normal, and it's the price of correctness: without it, the same combinations would still arise, just not inside a separate table under control, but inside a calculation, multiplying sums. Both source tables connect to the bridge as one-to-many, and the key no longer repeats on either of the two relationships.

options.label: One row is one "this product belongs to this promo's brand" pair. 465 is the sum, across brands, of products times promos — for «Nettora» that's 5 × 10 = 50
options.why: A bridge lists every valid combination explicitly. Within a brand, every one of its products pairs with every one of its promos, so a brand's contribution is a product of two counts, and the total size is the sum of those products across all nine brands.

options.label: One row is one brand with a list of its products and promos. 465 is the total number of brand mentions across both tables
options.why: A list inside a row would mean one cell holds a list — that isn't how a relational table works. A bridge lays combinations out one per row, which is exactly why there end up being more of them than rows in the original lookups.

options.label: One row is one product with its most recent promo. 465 is the number of products times the number of months of history
options.why: Picking the "most recent" promo would drop all the others and turn the relationship back into one-to-many, with data loss along the way. The whole point of a bridge is to keep every combination, not pick one.

options.label: 465 is 47 products plus 89 promos plus 329 sales that fell under a promo
options.why: A bridge links two lookups and knows nothing about sales — the fact table connects to the model separately, via promo_id. Adding up the rows of two tables also doesn't give you their relationship's cardinality: that's set by combinations, not a sum.

tasks.title: The bridge's row sum exceeds the total
tasks.brief: The bridge is built, the relationships are set. On a by-promo report, the sum of revenue across every row turns out bigger than the sales table's grand total.
tasks.goal: Work out whether this is a bug or expected behaviour.
tasks.scenario:
Report: rows are promos,
measure is the promo's brand
revenue.

Sum across every row:
more than ¥126,911,191
(fact_sellout's full total)

The report's Total row:
exactly ¥126,911,191.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why is the sum of the rows bigger than the total, while the total itself is correct?
hints: Remember mdl-021: the Total row computes in its own filter context, it doesn't sum what's visible above it.
Can one sale belong to several promos of the same brand at once?
tasks.explain: A many-to-many relationship inherently produces overlapping breakdowns: the same fact belongs to several elements of a dimension at once. So the sum of the visible rows and the Total row legitimately diverge — they're computed in different filter contexts, and the total doesn't sum the rows, it recomputes the measure with no promo condition. This isn't a defect of the bridge, it's a property of the relationship it honestly describes. The practical takeaway for an analyst: on reports with m2m breakdowns, either keep the Total row and explain it, or drop it entirely — but never "fix" it by dividing, since dividing changes the measure's meaning rather than correcting an error. And it's worth checking the question itself separately: if the business genuinely needs revenue for a specific promo, the breakdown should be built on promo_id, where there's no duplication at all.

options.label: Expected: a brand has several promos, and its revenue lands in the row of every one of them. The total is recomputed with no per-promo breakdown, so it doesn't double-count
options.why: Through the bridge, one sale belongs to several promos of the same brand, and its revenue legitimately shows up in every such row. The Total row lives in a different filter context — with no promo condition — so it counts every sale exactly once.

options.label: A bridge bug: duplicate pairs are left in it, and that's doubling the revenue
options.why: The pairs in the bridge are unique — otherwise it wouldn't do its job. The excess doesn't come from duplicates — it comes from the same product honestly belonging to several different promos of its brand.

options.label: A measure bug: revenue needs dividing by the brand's promo count, so the rows sum to the total
options.why: Dividing would turn an understandable quantity ("revenue of the brand this promo belonged to") into a share whose meaning would need explaining separately. If the business genuinely needs a non-duplicating sum, what needs to change is the question, not the measure — compute by promo_id, not by brand.

options.label: A total bug: it should equal the sum of the rows, or the report shouldn't be shown
options.why: The rule "total equals the sum of the rows" only holds for additive measures across non-overlapping breakdowns. Here the breakdown overlaps by construction, and a total recomputed in its own context is actually more honest than a mechanical sum.

tasks.title: CALCULATE isn't WHERE
tasks.brief: A measure computes brand «Aqualis»'s revenue. Someone puts a slicer for brand «Nettora» on the page — two different brands at once.
tasks.goal: Work out what the measure returns.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does the measure return with a slicer on a different brand?
hints: The key word is "replaces." What survives of the brand slicer once CALCULATE applies its own condition to the same column?
Check it on a different column: if the slicer were on region and the condition on brand, both would stay in effect.
tasks.explain: This is the main difference between CALCULATE and WHERE, and the source of most confusion when reading someone else's measures. WHERE adds a condition to whatever's already there; CALCULATE replaces the filter on the column it mentions, and leaves filters on other columns alone. The practical consequence: a measure with a baked-in brand condition will keep showing the same brand no matter what's chosen in a brand slicer — but it will honestly narrow under a region or date slicer. If you actually need an intersection — keep the external filter and add your own condition on top — there's KEEPFILTERS, which changes CALCULATE's behaviour to exactly that: combining conditions.

options.label: «Aqualis»'s full revenue — ¥18,841,733. The condition inside CALCULATE replaced the brand filter, rather than adding to it
options.why: CALCULATE doesn't intersect its condition with an existing filter on the same column — it replaces it. The «Nettora» slicer disappears for this measure entirely, and it computes as if there were no brand slicer at all.

options.label: Zero — a product can't be both «Aqualis» and «Nettora» at once, the intersection is empty
options.why: No intersection happens: that's how WHERE behaves in SQL, where conditions combine with AND. CALCULATE works differently — its condition on a column displaces whatever was already set on that column.

options.label: «Nettora»'s revenue — ¥16,165,815, because the page slicer takes priority over the measure's formula
options.why: The priority runs the other way: a filter set inside CALCULATE applies after the external context and overwrites it on its own column. That's exactly why a measure with a baked-in condition behaves the same regardless of slicers on that same column.

options.label: The sum of both brands — ¥35,007,548, because the conditions combine with OR
options.why: No combining happens either. CALCULATE doesn't combine its condition with the external one via AND or OR — it fully replaces the filter on that column, leaving filters on every other column untouched.

tasks.title: The filter on a different column survives
tasks.brief: The same measure with a baked-in brand, but now the page slicer is by region, not brand — «Tokyo».
tasks.goal: Work out which filters act on the calculation.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does the measure return with a region slicer?
hints: Compare with mdl-037: there the condition and the slicer were on the same column, here they're on different ones.
CALCULATE replaces filters selectively. On which columns exactly?
tasks.explain: This shows the other half of the rule, without which the first half looks alarming. CALCULATE doesn't "break the context" wholesale — it acts precisely, only on the columns mentioned in its conditions. Filters on every other column pass straight through and combine with the measure's condition. This is exactly what makes measures with baked-in conditions practically useful: "Aqualis Revenue" stays «Aqualis»'s revenue under any brand slicer, while still honestly breaking down by region, month and channel. To remove the external filter entirely you need an explicit ALL — a different technique, with a different meaning and different consequences.

options.label: ¥1,323,959 — «Aqualis»'s revenue in Tokyo. Both filters apply: brand from the measure, region from the slicer
options.why: CALCULATE only replaces the filter on the columns its conditions mention. Brand and region are different columns of different tables, so the brand condition did nothing to the region slicer, and both narrowed the calculation at once.

options.label: ¥18,841,733 — «Aqualis»'s full revenue, because CALCULATE wipes out the entire external context
options.why: CALCULATE doesn't wipe the entire context — only filters on the columns it mentions. Wiping the whole external filter takes an explicit instruction, ALL for instance, and that's exactly the difference between "replace the brand filter" and "remove every filter."

options.label: ¥8,876,489 — all of Tokyo's revenue, because the page slicer beats the condition in the formula
options.why: The formula's condition applies on top of the external context and wins on its own column. The region slicer survives not because it's stronger, but because it's about a different column, and there's simply no conflict with it.

tasks.title: The share that's always a hundred percent
tasks.brief: A brand-share measure returns 100% in every row of a by-brand matrix. The formula looks correct: revenue divided by revenue.
tasks.goal: Work out the cause and how to fix it.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why is the share 100%, and what needs to change?
hints: In the «Fruvia» row, what are the numerator and denominator individually?
The denominator needs a context with no brand filter. Which function removes a filter from a column?
tasks.explain: Any share is a ratio of a value in the current context to a value in a wider one, and the whole difficulty is setting that wider context explicitly. Without CALCULATE, both halves of the formula live in the same row-level filter context and give identical numbers. ALL removes the filter from the specified column, giving the denominator full reach: in the «Fruvia» row the numerator stays ¥25,465,980, the denominator becomes ¥126,911,191, and the share comes out to 20.1%. Notice the difference from the constant in mdl-017: ALL recomputes along with every other slicer — filter by Tokyo and the denominator becomes Tokyo's revenue, and the shares still sum to a hundred percent. That's exactly why shares are written with ALL, not a hard-coded number.

options.label: The numerator and denominator compute in the same row-level filter context. The denominator needs freeing from the brand filter, via CALCULATE with ALL
options.why: In the «Fruvia» row, both halves of the formula see the same filter and both give ¥25,465,980 — the ratio is inevitably one. The denominator needs a different context: CALCULATE(SUM(revenue), ALL(dim_product[brand])) removes the brand filter and gives the full ¥126,911,191.

options.label: A DIVIDE bug: shares need a special percentage-calculating function
options.why: DIVIDE has nothing to do with it — it honestly divides whatever it's handed. The problem is that it was handed two identical numbers, and no other division function would change that.

options.label: The denominator needs replacing with the constant 126911191 — total revenue across the database
options.why: That gives a correct result right up to the first slicer: with a region filter, the numerator narrows while the hard-coded constant stays the same, and the shares stop summing to 100%. That's exactly the mistake covered in mdl-017.

options.label: The matrix is built wrong: shares should be computed at the visual level, not the measure level
options.why: A visual can show percent-of-total with a built-in setting, but that only solves the display case. A measure with ALL gives a quantity usable anywhere — inside another measure, in conditional formatting, in a value filter.

tasks.title: The same formula, two different numbers
tasks.brief: The formula SUM(revenue) is written twice: once as a measure, once as a calculated column in the product lookup. In a by-brand matrix they give different results.
tasks.goal: Work out why the results diverge.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why do a measure and a column with an identical formula give different numbers?
hints: Remember mdl-022: SUM inside a calculated column aggregates the whole table. What's different for a measure?
Invoking a measure is always implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE. What does CALCULATE do to row context?
tasks.explain: This is exactly where the two kinds of context meet. Row context gives a formula access to the current row's values, but aggregating functions don't read it — they only look at filter context. Context transition turns one into the other: inside CALCULATE, the current row becomes a filter, "every row where the key columns match." Invoking a measure is implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE, so a measure in a matrix automatically picks up the brand filter and gives ¥25,465,980. A calculated column has no such wrapping — its SUM sees an empty filter and aggregates everything, ¥126,911,191 in every one of the lookup's 47 rows. To make a column behave like a measure, wrapping its formula in CALCULATE by hand is enough.

options.label: Invoking a measure is implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE, and row context turns into a filter "brand = «Fruvia»." The column has no such transition, and SUM aggregates the whole table
options.why: Context transition happens inside CALCULATE, and invoking any measure is implicitly wrapped in it. So a measure in a matrix row sees the brand filter, while a calculated column doesn't: it has row context, but SUM doesn't respond to it.

options.label: The column computes at data refresh and the measure at display time, so the column's data is stale
options.why: The difference isn't about timing — that would matter for changing data, but here the data is identical. The gap would exist right after a refresh too: the column aggregates the whole table by the very nature of its context.

options.label: The measure is wrong: 25,465,980 is the revenue of just one «Fruvia» product, not the whole brand
options.why: ¥25,465,980 is the whole «Fruvia» brand's revenue, and that's the correct number for a brand row. It's the column that's wrong — showing ¥126,911,191, the full database total, in every row of the lookup indiscriminately.

options.label: A column can't reference another table, so it returns a default total
options.why: A column can reference another table — the relationship between dim_product and fact_sellout exists and works. The problem isn't data access — it's that SUM without CALCULATE is bounded by nothing except filter context, and the column has none.

tasks.title: A measure inside an iterator
tasks.brief: You need to count how many brands crossed ten million in revenue. The formula iterates brands and invokes a measure inside the iteration.
tasks.goal: Work out what the measure sees at each step of the iteration.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does [Total Revenue] compute at each step of FILTER?
hints: SUMX isn't an ordinary aggregating function like SUM — it's an iterator: it walks rows one at a time.
Ask: who creates row context in this example — a calculated column (like mdl-022), or FILTER itself?
tasks.explain: The "iterator plus a measure inside" construction is DAX's workhorse, and it rests entirely on context transition. FILTER iterates brands, creating a row context for each; invoking [Total Revenue] inside it is implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE, and that CALCULATE translates the row context into a filter, "brand = current." The measure computes exactly that brand's revenue, the condition compares it to the threshold, and FILTER keeps only the ones that qualify. Without context transition, formulas like this would be impossible: the measure would return the same total on every step. The practical tell for spotting this in someone else's code: if a measure is invoked inside an iterator, or there's an explicit CALCULATE, context transition is definitely happening, and the result needs reading with that in mind.

options.label: FILTER itself creates a row context for every row of fact_sellout and evaluates the expression passed to it inside that context — before summing the results at the end
options.why: FILTER creates a row context for each brand, and invoking a measure inside it is implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE — meaning context transition happens. The current brand becomes a filter, and the measure returns exactly that brand's revenue, not the grand total.

options.label: The grand total ¥126,911,191 on every step — the measure doesn't know what iteration it was invoked inside
options.why: If that were true, the condition would hold for all nine brands at once, and the formula would always return nine. It's exactly context transition that makes constructions like this meaningful: a measure inside an iterator sees the current element of the iteration.

options.label: Zero on every step — VALUES returns a list of brands with no connection to the fact table
options.why: VALUES returns a column's values, and the relationship between dim_product and fact_sellout doesn't go anywhere. The brand filter that context transition produces travels along that relationship into the fact table in the ordinary way.

options.label: The first brand's revenue alphabetically — FILTER evaluates the condition once and applies it to everyone
options.why: FILTER is an iterator — it evaluates the condition fresh for every row of the table being iterated. Evaluating once would make filtering pointless: the result wouldn't depend on which rows are being iterated at all.

tasks.title: A column that behaves like a measure
tasks.brief: A calculated column in the product lookup needs to show its own product's revenue, not the grand total.
tasks.goal: Work out which formula fix solves this.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which variant gives exactly its own product's revenue?
hints: Context transition is the work of CALCULATE itself. Does it need conditions to do that?
Check RELATED's direction: which side of the relationship does it look from, and which does it look toward?
tasks.explain: CALCULATE with no conditions looks pointless, and that's why it's rarely recognized in someone else's code, even though it does something quite specific: it performs context transition. The lookup's current row turns into a filter, "product = this one", SUM inside it sees only that product's sales, and the column starts behaving like a measure. That's exactly why experienced authors sometimes write CALCULATE around an aggregate with not a single argument — it isn't a forgotten condition, it's a deliberate switch of context type. It's worth remembering the cost too: a column like this computes once at refresh and freezes its result, so in most cases keeping a measure is the better call, and setting up a column only makes sense when the value genuinely needs to stay fixed — to filter or sort by it afterward, for instance.

options.label: Variant A — CALCULATE with not a single condition still performs context transition: the lookup row becomes a filter, "this product"
options.why: Context transition is the job of CALCULATE itself, not of its conditions. Even an empty CALCULATE turns the current row into a filter, and SUM inside it starts seeing only that product's sales. This is the idiomatic way to get measure-like behaviour in a column.

options.label: Variant B — RELATED fetches the related value from the fact table
options.why: RELATED works in the opposite direction: it pulls a value from the "one" side to the "many" side — meaning from a lookup into a fact table. It doesn't look from lookup into fact at all — there, one lookup row corresponds to many fact rows, and a single value simply doesn't exist.

options.label: Variant C — SUMX iterates the fact table row by row and so sees only its own rows
options.why: SUMX will create a row context for every row of fact_sellout, but it will iterate the whole table regardless: there's no filter for the current product, because no context transition happened. The result stays the same grand total, just computed more expensively.

tasks.title: What YTD does to the filter
tasks.brief: A by-month matrix has a year-to-date revenue measure. In the March 2025 row it shows more than March's own revenue.
tasks.goal: Work out where the bigger number comes from.
tasks.predictQuestion: What did TOTALYTD do to the date filter?
hints: Compare 12,566,159 to the sum of January, February and March 2025's revenue. Does it match?
Every time intelligence function is a wrapper around CALCULATE. What does CALCULATE do to a filter?
tasks.explain: Time intelligence functions look like a separate mechanism, but they're built the same simple way: each is a wrapper around CALCULATE, swapping the calendar filter for a different set of dates. TOTALYTD replaces the current period with the interval from the start of the year to the end of the current one, and SUM(revenue) computes over it exactly the way it would over any other filter. There's no stored cumulative column anywhere in the model — which is exactly why the measure stays correct when any other slicer gets added: apply a region filter, and YTD recomputes for that region. Understanding it as "just swapping dates" removes the need to memorize each function individually — it's enough to know what interval it changes the filter to.

options.label: Replaced the "March 2025" filter with "January 1st through March 31st, 2025" — meaning January, February and March together
options.why: TOTALYTD is a wrapper around CALCULATE that swaps the calendar filter for the interval from the start of the year to the end of the current period. The underlying data stays the same: ¥12,566,159 is the sum of three months' revenue, not some other quantity.

options.label: Added prior years' data for the same month to the March filter
options.why: That's what a different function does — SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR — and it would return March 2024, meaning ¥4,392,846. TOTALYTD works within the current year and never crosses its boundary.

options.label: Didn't change the filter — it pulled a stored cumulative value from a separate column in the model
options.why: No such separate column exists — all time intelligence computes on the fly from the same SUM(revenue). That's exactly why measures like this work correctly under any additional slicer: they don't store pre-computed totals.

options.label: Multiplied March's revenue by the month number to get a cumulative total
options.why: Multiplying would give ¥14,082,990, with no relation to the actual January and February data. A cumulative total is always the actual sum for the interval, never an estimate off an average.

tasks.title: Comparing to last year
tasks.brief: You need month-over-month growth against last year. The measure compares the current period's revenue to the same period a year earlier.
tasks.goal: Work out what the measure returns in the March 2025 row.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does RevenueLY show in the March 2025 row, and what growth does that imply?
hints: The function shifts the set of dates back a year, preserving the period's length. What does March 2025 become?
Check the edge case: what does this measure return in the January 2024 row?
tasks.explain: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR takes the dates from the current filter and shifts them back a year, preserving the period's length and position: March gives March, a quarter gives a quarter. CALCULATE then computes the expression over the new set of dates. This produces an important edge case people forget on a first implementation: in the model's earliest period, there is no prior year, and the measure returns blank — in our dataset that's all of 2024, which has no 2023 to compare to. On a report this shows up as a hole in the first row, and it needs either an explanation or explicit handling. The second condition for correct behaviour is a continuous calendar marked in the model as a date table: the shift is computed by date arithmetic, and a gap in the calendar silently breaks it.

options.label: ¥4,392,846 — March 2024's revenue. Growth comes to 6.9%
options.why: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR takes the dates caught by the current filter and shifts them back exactly a year, after which CALCULATE computes over the new set. The ratio of 4,694,330 to 4,392,846 gives roughly 6.9% growth.

options.label: ¥4,694,330 — the same March 2025 revenue, because the measure computes off the same fact table
options.why: The fact table really is the same, but the date filter has been swapped — that's the whole point of the function. An identical result would mean the shift didn't work, and the usual cause of that is an incomplete date lookup, or one not marked as a date table.

options.label: ¥49,518,071 — all of 2024's revenue, because SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts the filter to the entire year
options.why: The function preserves the period's length and position — it doesn't expand it to a full year. From March 2025 it makes March 2024, from Q1 it makes last year's Q1, and a full year would only come out of a full year.

options.label: Blank — there's no data for March 2024, because the model starts in 2025
options.why: Data starts on January 1st 2024 and covers two and a half years. It would be blank for January 2024, where the model genuinely has no prior year — and that's an important edge case worth checking in the first row of any report like this.

tasks.title: A calendar with gaps
tasks.brief: A colleague built the date table from dates that actually appear in sales: SELECT DISTINCT week_start. YTD behaves strangely on it.
tasks.goal: Work out why a calendar like this breaks time intelligence.
tasks.scenario:
Calendar built from facts:
  only dates that had sales

Correct dim_date:
  912 consecutive days,
  2024-01-01 to 2026-06-30,
  all 365 days of 2025

The model has a product
launched in September 2025.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why does a fact-derived calendar break time intelligence functions?
hints: A product launched in September 2025 — which days had no sales for it, and would those days even make it into a fact-derived calendar?
How does a function compute "the same period a year ago" — by looking up a neighbouring row, or by date arithmetic?
tasks.explain: A calendar for an analytical model isn't derived from facts — it's an independent lookup table that must be continuous and cover complete years. Time intelligence functions build a new set of dates by computation, not by navigating rows, so any gap shifts the interval's boundaries and silently understates the result. In our model, dim_date holds 912 consecutive days, including ones with no sales at all: for a product launched in September 2025, the January days of that same year are still in the calendar, and YTD computes correctly. The check takes a second: the calendar's row count should equal the difference between its earliest and latest dates, plus one. There's an extra condition too: the calendar has to be marked in the model as a date table, or some functions will refuse to work even on continuous data.

options.label: They compute the prior period by date arithmetic, not by looking up a neighbouring row. A missing day silently shifts the interval's boundaries
options.why: Functions like SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and TOTALYTD build a new set of dates by computation — shifting by a year, counting from the start of the year. If some days are missing from the calendar, the interval comes out incomplete, and the result silently ends up smaller than the real one, with no warning at all.

options.label: A calendar like this contains duplicates, because one week appears in the facts many times
options.why: DISTINCT is exactly what removes repeats, so there won't be duplicates in a table like this. The problem is the opposite — not extra rows, but missing ones: days with no sales never make it into the calendar at all.

options.label: The functions require the calendar to hold future dates at least a year ahead
options.why: The requirement for a calendar is continuity and complete years within the model, not a buffer into the future. A calendar ending today works perfectly fine, as long as there are no gaps inside it.

options.label: It's purely a performance problem: iterating dates off the fact table is slower than off a lookup
options.why: Speed isn't the main issue here. A 912-row calendar is small regardless; the danger is that an incomplete calendar gives wrong numbers, not slow ones.

tasks.title: One outlet, four spellings
tasks.brief: In the raw staging layer, the name of one and the same retail outlet is written several different ways. The by-outlet report shows it four times, splitting its revenue between the variants.
tasks.goal: Work out where this should be fixed.
tasks.scenario:
staging_raw_sellout, 3,110 rows.
One outlet appears as:

  «Ichiba #1026»
  «  Ichiba #1026 »
  «Itiba #1026»
  «  Itiba #1026 »

Differences: Ichiba/Itiba romanisation
and leading/trailing spaces.
tasks.predictQuestion: Where should this be cleaned, and why not in a measure?
hints: Ask: does the result of this cleanup depend on what is selected in the report slicers?
Think not only about the number in a measure, but about what a person sees in the filter list.
tasks.explain: The rule for choosing where to clean comes down to one question: does the result depend on the evaluation context. Normalising «Itiba» and «Ichiba» to a single form depends on no slicer at all, so it belongs in the preparation layer — in Power Query, or in the source itself if you have any influence there. What stays in a measure is only what evaluates differently under different filters. Cleaning in Power Query has a second advantage people forget: it fixes not only the numbers but the value lists in slicers — a person sees one «Ichiba» instead of four. A measure cannot do that in principle, because a filter is built from the model's data, not from measure formulas.

options.label: In Power Query at load time: the result does not depend on what is selected in the report, and it should be computed once before the data ever enters the model
options.why: Normalising spellings is an operation on the data itself, not on the result of a calculation: its outcome is identical under any slicer. Cleaned at load time, the outlet becomes a single lookup row, and no measure ever knows this problem existed.

options.label: In the measure, wrapping the name in TRIM and SUBSTITUTE — that way the fix needs no model refresh
options.why: It needs no refresh, true, but it repeats in every measure the outlet appears in, and one day those copies will disagree. Worse: the outlet slicer will still show four «Ichiba» entries — a measure fixes its own calculation, not what the person sees in the filter list.

options.label: Nowhere: this is the data as it is, and changing it distorts the source
options.why: Normalising the spellings of one entity is not distortion but the restoration of meaning: four strings describe one physical outlet. Merging genuinely different outlets would be distortion; here the differences are purely orthographic.

options.label: In the report visual, by configuring a grouping of similar values
options.why: Grouping in a visual solves the problem for one specific report and does not carry over to the others. It is also brittle: a fifth spelling appears, silently falls outside the group, and splits the revenue again.

tasks.title: Four date formats in one column
tasks.brief: In the raw staging layer, the sale-date column is filled in four different ways. The model loads it as text, and any work with dates breaks.
tasks.goal: Work out the order of operations when untangling a column like this.
tasks.scenario:
staging_raw_sellout, 3,110 rows,
column sale_date:

  ISO     2025-03-17   893
  dots    17.03.2025   803
  slashes 03/17/2025   764
  short   17.03.25     650

In the units column, numbers
are stored as text: "2", "6".
tasks.predictQuestion: What matters most to settle before converting these dates to a date type?
hints: Look at 03/17/2025 and imagine 07 in place of 17. How many readings appear?
Which error is worse: the one that breaks the load, or the one that yields a valid but wrong date?
tasks.explain: Mixed date formats are classic preparation-layer work, and the main danger in it is semantic rather than technical. The ISO and dotted formats are unambiguous: they can be parsed by rule and the result checked. The slashed format is ambiguous in principle — 03/07/2025 is both July 3rd and March 7th — and the data itself gives no answer. This is the case where the analyst's right move lies outside the tool: find out from the source's owner which convention applies there, and record the answer in a comment on the load step. The error is especially treacherous because it does not fail: the dates come out valid, the report builds, and the discrepancy surfaces months later during a reconciliation with someone else's system.

options.label: What 03/17/2025 means — which of the two numbers is the month. The slashed format is ambiguous, and getting the order wrong yields wrong dates wherever both numbers are twelve or less
options.why: March 17th parses unambiguously only because 17 cannot be a month. But in something like 03/07/2025 both readings are valid — July 3rd and March 7th — and the choice is settled by the source's convention, not by the data. The error here is silent: the dates come out valid, just not the right ones.

options.label: What type to give the units column — text or number: without that the dates will not parse
options.why: The types of units and sale_date are independent, and the order in which they are handled does not matter. Parsing the dates gets neither easier nor harder depending on whether units has been converted — that is a separate job in the same preparation layer.

options.label: How many rows are in each format — so you can keep the most common one and discard the rest
options.why: None of them can be discarded: all four formats describe genuine sales, and losing 2,217 rows out of 3,110 would distort any total. Every variant has to be parsed, not chosen between.

options.label: Whether a single "change type" step is enough: if not, the column is better left as text
options.why: Leaving it as text means losing all work with dates: no sorting, no relationship to the calendar, no time intelligence. Mixed formats can always be parsed; the only questions are how many steps it takes and whether the ambiguity has been resolved.

tasks.title: The filter that never reached the database
tasks.brief: The load pulls five years of history, though the report only needs the last two. There is a date filter in the query, yet the refresh still takes twenty minutes.
tasks.goal: Work out what could have broken in the load.
tasks.scenario:
Load steps:

  1. Source (table in the DB)
  2. Parse dates from text
  3. Filter: year >= 2024

The refresh pulls every row and
filters on its own side.
tasks.predictQuestion: Why did the filter not reduce the volume of the load?
hints: The loader tries to translate the steps into a single SQL query against the source. Are all the steps translatable?
What happens to the steps that come after an untranslatable one?
tasks.explain: Query folding is the mechanism behind loads that look identical differing tenfold in time. As long as every step translates into SQL, the whole chain collapses into one query and the database returns a finished result. The first untranslatable step breaks the fold: it and everything after it run locally, which means the data has to be downloaded in full. Hence the practical rule about step order: everything that reduces volume — date filters, picking only the needed columns — goes as early as possible and is phrased so it translates into SQL. Text parsing, replacements and other operations SQL has no equivalent for get pushed to the end. In this case the year filter should have been expressed against the original text column before parsing — then the database would have returned just the two years needed.

options.label: Parsing dates from text runs inside the loader and does not translate into SQL. After a step like that the filter can no longer be sent to the database and is applied locally, to every downloaded row
options.why: As long as the steps are translatable into SQL, they fold into one query against the source and the database returns data already filtered. An untranslatable step breaks that chain: everything after it is computed on the loader's side, which means the data has to be downloaded in full first.

options.label: A year filter does not work on a text column; it needs to be written as a string comparison
options.why: By the time the filter runs, step 2 has already parsed the date, and comparing by year is correct. The problem is not that the filter failed — it worked and gave the right result — but where it was applied.

options.label: Twenty minutes is normal for five years; a filter never affects load speed
options.why: It affects it a great deal — but only if it reaches the source. A properly folded filter makes the database return far fewer rows, and that is exactly what keeps refresh times acceptable on large models.

options.label: Swap the filter and the date parsing around — then it will make it into the SQL
options.why: The instinct is right, but phrased this way the step will not work: you cannot filter by year before parsing, the column is still text. The fix is to express the condition so it translates into SQL before parsing — by comparing a substring, say, or filtering on the source column directly.

tasks.title: An outlet moved to another region
tasks.brief: A retail outlet changed regions: it used to be in «Tokyo», now it is listed in «Kanagawa». One field in the lookup table was updated.
tasks.goal: Work out what happens to last year's report.
tasks.scenario:
dim_customer — 144 outlets,
16 regions; an outlet has one
region — the current one.

Was:  outlet → «Tokyo»
Now:  outlet → «Kanagawa»

The report "sales by region
for 2024" is rebuilt.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does the 2024 report show after the lookup table is edited?
hints: Where is the region of a sale physically stored — in the fact row, or in the lookup table?
The report recomputes every time it is opened. Where does it get the region for a sale that happened a year ago?
tasks.explain: An ordinary lookup table answers the question "which region is this outlet in now" — and that is the only question it can answer. A report for last year asks a different one: "which region was it in at the time of the sale." The difference between these questions is invisible while nothing changes, and it surfaces silently on the day the lookup gets edited: the regional total changes retroactively, nothing breaks, nobody gets a warning. This is the same class of error as the frozen column in mdl-016, only mirrored — there a value failed to recompute when it should have, here it recomputed when it should not have. The fix is versioning the lookup table, where each state has its own period of validity and the fact references the version that was current on the date of the event.

options.label: This outlet's entire 2024 sales history moves to «Kanagawa», as if it had always been there
options.why: The fact stores a reference to the outlet, not to a region: the region is taken from the lookup table at the moment the report is built. The lookup only knows the current value, so the whole history is recomputed against it — silently and retroactively.

options.label: The 2024 report will not change: it was built against the old lookup and stores the region as saved
options.why: Nothing is saved — the report is recomputed every time it is opened, and the region is fetched from the lookup each time. That is precisely the problem: the past gets rewritten along with the lookup table.

options.label: This outlet's 2024 sales will disappear: the link to the old region is broken
options.why: The relationship runs through customer_id, which did not change — the sales are not going anywhere. Only the region they land in when grouped changes, and that is more dangerous than disappearing: a disappearance would be noticed immediately.

options.label: The model will refuse to refresh and demand a date for the change
options.why: An ordinary lookup table knows nothing about time at all — it has neither a date field nor a versioning mechanism. Demanding a change date is exactly what SCD2 does, but it has to be designed first: the model will not ask for it on its own.

tasks.title: A "previous region" column
tasks.brief: To avoid losing history, a colleague proposes adding a "previous region" column to the lookup table — then the old value would be preserved.
tasks.goal: Work out whether this actually solves the problem.
tasks.scenario:
Proposed in dim_customer:

  region_id       current
  prev_region_id  previous

The outlet moved twice:
  until 2024-06 — «Tokyo»
  until 2025-03 — «Kanagawa»
  now — «Osaka»
tasks.predictQuestion: What does this solution fail to solve?
hints: The outlet moved twice. How many states fit into two columns?
Take a sale from January 15th 2025. Which column determines its region, and how would you know?
tasks.explain: A "previous value" column is a tempting solution because it looks like a small edit. It breaks for two independent reasons, and the second matters more than the first. The obvious one: you cannot know the number of states in advance, and the second move already needs a third column. The non-obvious and fundamental one: even with a complete set of columns you cannot match a sale to a version, because the versions have no periods of validity. SCD2 solves both at once by changing not the set of columns but the shape of storage: a customer gets as many rows as they have had states, each with its own "valid from — valid to" interval, and the fact references whichever was current on the date of the event. The number of changes then stops mattering — the structure works the same for one move and for ten.

options.label: Neither: the first move is already lost, and more importantly, the column cannot answer which region was in effect on a specific sale date
options.why: Two columns cover one change, and there were two — «Tokyo» has already been pushed out. But even with a single move an unanswerable question remains: does a sale from January 15th 2025 belong to the "current" region or the "previous" one? Without validity dates there is no answer.

options.label: It solves it completely: a measure just picks the right column depending on the report year
options.why: You can only pick by year if you know when the move happened — and that information is not in the lookup table. And even if it were, a rule of "one column before this year, another after" falls apart on the second change.

options.label: The only thing it fails to solve is performance: two columns double the size of the lookup
options.why: A 144-row lookup table is the cheapest table in the model, and an extra column in it costs nothing. The problem here is purely semantic: the structure cannot answer the question it was built for.

options.label: It fails only in the case where the outlet moved back to its earlier region
options.why: Moving back is a special case of the same general problem: any third version pushes out the first. But even with no moves back, the construction does not work, because it does not know the dates, and so cannot match a sale to a version.

tasks.title: Not every attribute needs versioning
tasks.brief: After working through the region problem, the team decides to version the entire customer lookup table — every attribute across the board.
tasks.goal: Work out which attributes this is justified for.
tasks.scenario:
dim_customer attributes:

  region_id     region
  channel       sales channel
  chain_name    retail chain
  customer_name name
  opened_date   opening date

Business questions differ:
some ask "how it was then",
others "how it is now".
tasks.predictQuestion: What tells you whether an attribute should be versioned?
hints: Split changes into two kinds: "the object became different" and "we were describing it wrong".
What should happen to an old report if a typo in an outlet's name is corrected?
tasks.explain: SCD2 is not a mode you switch on for a whole lookup table — it is a decision made per attribute, and it follows from one question: does the change reflect a new state of the object, or correct an error in its description? Moving to another region and switching sales channel are new states: last year's report should show what was true then, otherwise history gets rewritten. A corrected typo in a name is a description error: it has to propagate across the entire history, otherwise the lists show two objects where there is one. Hence the standard practice: both kinds coexist in one lookup table, some attributes versioned (SCD2), others overwritten (SCD1). Telling them apart is work the analyst does with the business, not a technical default.

options.label: By whether old reports should change along with the attribute. Region and channel affect sales history — version those; a corrected typo in a name should change everywhere
options.why: The question is not technical but substantive: is a change to the attribute a new state of the object, or a correction of an error in its description? A new state needs a version so the past stays the past; a corrected typo has to propagate across the whole history, otherwise reports will carry two spellings of one outlet.

options.label: Every attribute should be versioned: you cannot know in advance which one will be needed historically
options.why: Every version multiplies the lookup table's rows and complicates every relationship with the fact table. Versioning typos is also harmful in substance: it permanently preserves the wrong spelling alongside the right one as two distinct objects.

options.label: By how often it changes: what changes often is expensive to version, so it should not be
options.why: Frequency determines the size of the lookup table, not the need for history. An attribute that changes often and matters for historical reporting needs versioning all the more — that is exactly where the drift accumulates fastest.

options.label: By data type: text attributes get versioned, numbers and keys do not
options.why: A data type says nothing about the meaning of a change. Region is stored as a numeric key and does need versioning, while a name is text — and for a typo correction, precisely no version is wanted.

tasks.title: The night no longer fits into the night
tasks.brief: The model does a full refresh every night and rereads the entire history. The refresh window has stopped fitting before morning.
tasks.goal: Work out what share of the work is done for nothing.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellout — 118,449 rows:

  2024   48,391
  2025   47,122
  2026   22,936

The last three months brought
11,353 rows.

History is not edited
after the fact.
tasks.predictQuestion: What share of the rows is worth rereading every night?
hints: How many of the 118,449 rows could have changed since last night, if history is not edited?
Note the condition in the task: history is not edited after the fact. What follows from that?
tasks.explain: Incremental refresh slices the fact table into partitions by date and rereads only those changes could have arrived in. The gain is directly proportional to the share of fresh data: 11,353 rows out of 118,449 means nine tenths of the nightly work is done for nothing. The key condition, without which none of this works, is hidden in the premise itself — history is not edited after the fact. That is exactly the statement to check with the business before configuring anything: the depth to which corrections genuinely arrive is what sets the boundary of the refreshed partitions. Getting it wrong here is dangerous because the drift shows up as neither an error nor a warning — the model simply spends years showing a version the source corrected long ago.

options.label: About a tenth — the 11,353 rows from the last three months. The other 107,000 have not changed and are reread for nothing
options.why: Only what changes could have arrived in needs refreshing. Given that history is not edited, that means the recent months: 11,353 rows out of 118,449 — less than a tenth of the work instead of all of it.

options.label: All 118,449 — otherwise the integrity of the model cannot be guaranteed
options.why: Integrity is provided by partitioning, not by rereading everything. Partitions for earlier years stay exactly as they were loaded, and their contents do not depend on whether they were refreshed that night.

options.label: Only 2026 — 22,936 rows, because partitions are conventionally annual
options.why: An annual partition is one option, not a rule. The boundary is chosen by how deep changes genuinely arrive: if history is not edited, three months is enough, and the work comes out half as large again.

options.label: Half — the last full year of data, as a safety margin against late corrections
options.why: A safety margin "just in case" costs exactly the volume that gets reread for nothing. It is better to find out the real depth of corrections from the business and set the boundary by it than to guess at a buffer.

tasks.title: The correction that never arrived
tasks.brief: Incremental refresh is configured for the last three months. An error in March 2025 sales was corrected in the source — nearly a year ago.
tasks.goal: Work out what the model shows after the next refresh.
tasks.scenario:
Partitions refreshed:
  last 3 months — yes
  anything earlier — no

A sale from March 2025 was
corrected in the source.

The refresh completed fine,
no errors in the log.
tasks.predictQuestion: What does the model show for March 2025 after the refresh?
hints: The model does not read the old partitions at all. How would it learn that something changed in the source?
Note that there are no errors in the log. Is that a good sign or a worrying one?
tasks.explain: Incremental refresh is a contract: history is immutable, therefore it need not be reread. As long as the contract holds, everything works. The moment old data gets corrected in the source, the model and the source diverge — and diverge silently, because there is no detection mechanism here by construction: any check would mean reading exactly what was decided not to read. Two practical consequences follow. First: the depth of refreshed partitions is set not by technical convenience but by the real depth of corrections in the business process. Second: when a retroactive correction does happen — and it does — you need a manual way to reload a specific partition, and that way has to be written down in advance, not invented at the moment the discrepancy is discovered.

options.label: The old, uncorrected value — the March 2025 partition was not refreshed, and the correction never reached the model. And there will be no sign of the discrepancy at all
options.why: A partition excluded from refresh lives on as a snapshot from its last load. The source and the model diverge silently: the refresh ran normally over its own partitions, the log is clean, and the number in the report stayed as it was.

options.label: The new value — the model compares partition checksums and pulls in the one that changed
options.why: No checksum comparison happens: the whole point of the mechanism is not to touch the old partitions at all. Any check of their contents would require exactly the reading the whole thing was set up to avoid.

options.label: The refresh will fail with a data mismatch error
options.why: There is nothing to fail on — the model does not know anything changed in the source and does not try to find out. The absence of an error is the real danger here: the discrepancy looks like normal operation.

options.label: Blank — the March 2025 partition will be flagged as stale and excluded from reports
options.why: There is no staleness flag on partitions, and the data does not disappear. The partition keeps taking part in reports on equal terms with the rest, just with the contents it had at its last load.

tasks.title: Where the partition boundary runs
tasks.brief: Incremental refresh is being configured. You need to pick the column to slice the table into partitions by — and the shipments fact has two dates.
tasks.goal: Work out which column is suitable for partitioning.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellin, two dates:

  order_date  order date
  ship_date   shipment date,
              2-11 days later

1,979 orders out of 15,362
ship in the following month.

The order creates the row,
shipment is filled in later.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which date should partitions be sliced by, and why does it matter?
hints: A partition is determined when the row is loaded. Which of the two dates is already known by then and will never change?
Picture a row loaded on March 30th with an empty shipment date. Where does it end up when the shipment is filled in on April 4th?
tasks.explain: The column used for partitioning has to have one property that is easy to overlook: it must be known the moment the row appears and never change afterward. order_date qualifies — an order is dated when it is created. ship_date gets filled in later, and a row already placed in the March partition would formally need to move to the April one; the mechanism does not support such a move, and the result is data sitting in the wrong partition, which breaks both the refresh and date filtering. The general rule: partition by the date of the event that creates the row, not by the date of its later processing. If reporting is needed specifically by shipment date, that is solved by a role-playing calendar (see the inactive relationship and USERELATIONSHIP), not by the choice of partitioning column.

options.label: By order_date — a row lands in its partition once and never changes it. Partitioning by ship_date means a row can move between partitions when the shipment is filled in
options.why: A partition is determined at the moment the row is loaded. order_date is known immediately and does not change, so the row stays in its partition forever. ship_date is filled in later — a row loaded as a March one would have to end up in the April partition once shipment is recorded, and the mechanism has no provision for such a move.

options.label: By ship_date — a shipment is a completed event, whereas an order can be cancelled
options.why: How complete an event is matters for the meaning of a report, but not for partitioning. What is critical for partitions is a different property — immutability: the column must determine the partition once and for all, otherwise rows start migrating between partitions.

options.label: By either — partitions get rebuilt on every refresh anyway
options.why: Partitions specifically do not get rebuilt — that is the entire point of the mechanism: the old ones stay untouched. Which is exactly why the choice of column is irreversible and determines correctness for the whole life of the model.

options.label: By both at once — build a two-dimensional partitioning to cover either scenario
options.why: Two-dimensional partitioning multiplies the number of partitions sharply and complicates maintenance without solving the original problem: a row would still migrate along one of the dimensions once the shipment was recorded.

tasks.title: The most expensive column
tasks.brief: The model takes up too much memory. You need to work out which column of the fact table costs the most.
tasks.goal: Identify the most expensive column and the reason.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellout — 118,449 rows.
Distinct values per column:

  sellout_id   118,449
  revenue       86,389
  units            154
  week_start       131
  product_id        47
tasks.predictQuestion: Which column takes up the most space, and why?
hints: The engine compresses a column better the fewer distinct values it holds. Where are there most of them?
Ask of every column: does anyone display it in a report or filter by it?
tasks.explain: A columnar store compresses data by replacing values with references into a dictionary of distinct values. The smaller the dictionary, the tighter the compression: product_id with 47 values is stored almost for free, week_start with 131 nearly so. A column where every value is unique has no dictionary at all and is stored as is, becoming the most expensive one in the table. A row surrogate key is the classic example of such a column — and at the same time it is entirely useless in a report: nobody groups or filters by a row identifier. Removing it from the model is the cheapest optimisation available: a noticeable memory win with not a single capability lost. A habit worth forming: before discussing how much history to keep, sort the columns by distinct-value count and check whether everything at the top is genuinely needed by the report.

options.label: sellout_id — 118,449 distinct values across 118,449 rows. A column where every value is unique does not compress at all, and the report never needs it once
options.why: The engine stores data by column and compresses it by replacing repeated values with references into a dictionary. A row surrogate key has no repeats, so the dictionary equals the column itself and compression gains nothing. Meanwhile a row surrogate key is never displayed in a report or filtered by.

options.label: week_start — dates take more space than numbers, and there are 131 distinct values
options.why: 131 distinct values across 118,449 rows is excellent compressibility: a 131-entry dictionary and short references into it. The data type is secondary here; what decides is the number of distinct values.

options.label: revenue — 86,389 values and a fractional type, the most expensive of the lot
options.why: revenue really is the second most expensive column, and it is worth discussing — rounding to kopecks or to whole roubles if that precision is not needed. But at least it is used in reports, unlike a row identifier.

options.label: All roughly the same: space is determined by row count, and that is identical for every column
options.why: The row count is identical, the space is not: a column with 47 distinct values compresses many times better than one with 118,449. That is exactly why shrinking a model starts with columns, not with rows.

tasks.title: Trimming history for the sake of size
tasks.brief: The model needs to be smaller. The proposal is to drop 2024 — that would cut the rows almost in half.
tasks.goal: Work out the real effect of such a decision.
tasks.scenario:
fact_sellout — 118,449 rows:
  2024  48,391
  2025  47,122
  2026  22,936

Drop 2024 and:
  70,058 rows remain (−41%)

Prices, amounts and products
repeat across years.
tasks.predictQuestion: How much smaller does the model get, and what is lost?
hints: How many distinct products remain after dropping a year? And how many were there before?
Which matters more to the business — freeing memory, or keeping the ability to compute growth against last year?
tasks.explain: Trimming history is intuitively the most obvious way to shrink a model and almost always the least rewarding. A column's weight is made up of its dictionary of distinct values plus the references into it; deleting rows only reduces the second part, while the first — the bulk of the weight for expensive columns — stays nearly untouched, because values repeat across years. What gets given up in exchange is year-over-year comparison, which is exactly the capability history is kept for. The right order is the reverse: first remove columns that appear in no report (see mdl-055), then reduce precision where it is excessive — rounding amounts, for instance — and only then, if that was not enough, discuss the depth of history with the business as a deliberate trade-off.

options.label: Noticeably less than 41%: the number of distinct values in the expensive columns barely changes. And year-over-year comparison is lost for good
options.why: Size is determined by dictionaries of distinct values, and those overlap between years: the same 47 products, largely repeating prices and amounts. Rows drop by 41%, dictionaries barely shrink. In exchange, the ability to compute growth against last year disappears — the single most common request in reporting.

options.label: Exactly 41% — however many rows you removed, that much space is freed
options.why: There is no direct proportion between rows and size in a columnar store. The references into the dictionary do shrink proportionally, but the dictionaries themselves — the bulk of the weight of the expensive columns — stay nearly as they were.

options.label: More than 41%: deleting rows also improves compression of the ones left
options.why: Compression of the remaining data does not improve when neighbouring rows are removed — dictionaries are built from the values that remain. There is no gain to expect beyond the share of rows deleted.

options.label: It will not shrink at all: a columnar store does not depend on row count
options.why: The dependency exists, it is just not linear: there will be proportionally fewer references into the dictionary. There is a gain, it is simply far more modest than the share of deleted rows suggests.

tasks.title: Precision you pay for
tasks.brief: After removing the row identifier the model is still a bit large. Next up is the second most expensive column — revenue, with 86,389 distinct values.
tasks.goal: Work out how to reduce its weight without losing meaning.
tasks.scenario:
revenue — 86,389 distinct
values across 118,449 rows.

Values look like:
  398.31   399.28   601.40

Reports show revenue in
thousands and millions of ¥;
kopecks appear nowhere.
tasks.predictQuestion: What reduces the column's weight without breaking the reports?
hints: What is a column's dictionary made of, and what in the value 398.31 multiplies it hardest?
Ask what precision the reports actually display. Does it match what is stored?
tasks.explain: After removing the obviously unneeded columns, the next technique is reducing precision where it is excessive. Kopecks in a revenue column nearly double the dictionary and take part in no report that shows totals in thousands: that is payment for precision nobody uses. Rounding at load time cuts the number of distinct values and changes not a single visible figure. What matters is that this is a deliberate trade-off, not a free optimisation: rounding is irreversible, and if a kopeck-level reconciliation with accounting is needed tomorrow, the data for it will no longer be in the model. So the decision is made together with the business and written down, not done silently. The general order for optimising a model: unneeded columns first, excessive precision second, and only last of all, the depth of history.

options.label: Round to whole roubles at load time: the number of distinct values drops, and reports that show revenue in thousands will not notice a thing
options.why: A column's dictionary consists of its distinct values, and kopecks multiply them almost for nothing: 398.31 and 398.47 are two dictionary entries for a difference no report displays. Rounding to whole roubles shrinks the dictionary and affects not one visible figure.

options.label: Delete the revenue column and compute revenue as units × price from the lookup table
options.why: List price and actual sale price are different quantities (see mdl-009): sales happen at discounts and on promotion. Such a calculation would give revenue without discounts — replacing a correct number with a wrong one to save memory.

options.label: Split revenue into two columns — roubles and kopecks separately, each with a smaller dictionary
options.why: The combined dictionary of the two columns will be no smaller, and working with revenue gets more complicated in every measure. The technique is occasionally used for very large numbers, but here it only adds complexity with no gain.

options.label: Do nothing: reports need revenue, so its weight is a mandatory cost
options.why: What is needed is not the whole column but its significant part. The cost is mandatory for the precision actually used, and kopecks in reports that deal in millions are never used.
